speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of an article appearing in this morning's Globe and Mail to the effect that the supply of mortgage money from chartered banks and insurance companies for National Housing Act financing of new houses has almost vanished across Canada, with millions of dollars' worth of applications being returned unapproved in recent weeks, that the worst hit are Ontario and Quebec, and that the builders describe the situation as bad and rapidly getting worse and that building may be at a standstill in Windsor and in the Toronto district, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether this tight-money policy announced by Mr. Coyne of the Bank of Canada is the considered policy of this government?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, arising out of the last answer may I ask the minister whether or not there is any foundation for the press release of two days ago to the effect that within the next three or four weeks, or possibly in about six weeks, there will be a reduction in interest rates in the Bank of Canada? subtopic: MORTGAGE MONEY

Well, Mr. Speaker, first of all there is no basis for the newspaper speculation that a reduction might occur; that is not to say that it would not, however. These matters are never forecast; they are only announced when they occur.
As to what the government is doing, since this question arose-I think it was brought to our attention about ten days or two weeks ago-my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) has been carefully considering the housing situation in Canada and we have been consulting with him and with the banks with respect to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ALLOCATION, MOVEMENT AND SHORTAGES OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I announced
earlier in the session that it would be impossible to follow the policy of last year in maintaining uniform deliveries at all country elevator points. I pointed out that this is an exceptional year in the movement of grain out of Canada and the only way to take full advantage of it is to move to terminals the type of grain for which there is a ready sale. That policy has been followed and at the moment a very definite effort is being made to bring points which now have a low quota up to the average quota for the three prairie provinces.
I am aware, as I said yesterday, that the Canadian National have moved a considerably greater proportion of the grain on their lines to terminals than has the Canadian Pacific. In the light of that fact, arrangements are being made so that the farmer who formerly delivered to a Canadian Pacific point and who is within trucking distance of a Canadian National point will have the option of delivering to alternate delivery points. In other words, if there is a low quota on the Canadian Pacific point and a high quota on the Canadian National point within trucking distance, the farmer may deliver to the high quota point.
This is one step that is being taken. As far as Canadian Pacific lines are concerned, every effort is being made to favour the low quota points. I am hopeful that there will be a definite improvement before the end of the crop year.
It is touch and go to keep the right kind of grain at ocean terminals. Boats are arriving in great numbers and they are arriving out of order. We may plan on loading No. 2 northern the following week, and perhaps No. 5 northern boats that had been expected earlier will suddenly arrive and we must have that grade of grain as well. It is a tremendous job, and I should mention the fine work of the transport controller in that connection. To date, whilst there has been some small amount of demurrage paid, he has succeeded very well indeed in having the kind of grain in hand that the boats require. But we have a situation on the lower St. Lawrence today that there is not enough
Inquiries of the Ministry grain in the elevators to take care of one week's loadings. In other words, we are unloading canalers to provide grain needed to load waiting ocean boats. Whilst we have not the same situation on the west coast, there it is quite a problem of having adequate stocks of the grades required to fill the ocean boats.
I think my hon. friend would agree with me that in a year like this the principal objective must be to deliver grain to our overseas customers in the largest possible quantities. If we are not able to even out the deliveries at every country elevator, we can compensate after August 1, for this abnormal movement promises to continue. We shall try to see that in the long run every producer gets an even break.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that every member of the house who has read the white paper and realizes the importance of this debate wants to say something in the debate, and I am no exception. So far as information is concerned, the white paper leaves much to be desired. Practically all members of the house are in the position of having very little personal knowledge of defence matters or whether the money is being spent judiciously or otherwise. Of course, the Minister of National Defence, who presides over the three defence branches, is also in the position where he must accept the information given to him by the heads of the different branches. He is not in a very much better position than we are when it comes to analysing the expenditures that are made and the value we are receiving for the money spent.
I know that the minister has three very efficient deputy ministers. I have done business with all three and they are very courteous, fast in their work, and will give you any information you are looking for within reason. But at the same time I have always been of the opinion that one of the main needs of the defence department and

one of the greatest assets that the Minister of National Defence could have is a continuing defence committee of the House of Commons. They have one in Britain and they also have one in the United States. In my opinion, whoever opposes the idea is doing the Minister of National Defence a disservice. In this house there are approximately 100 members who are ex-servicemen, army, navy and air force, and they could be very helpful to the minister if we had a continuing committee before which the heads of the departments could be called, in camera, if necessary, in order that we might get all the information they could give with respect to defence spending, obsolescence of equipment, progress in the future and so forth. I think even the fact that such a committee existed would be a deterrent to those in the different branches of the department who might be inclined to spend recklessly. In my opinion the fact that there was a committee before which they could be called would act as a very useful brake, and I think the opinions of members of the house with experience in the services would be valuable to the Minister of National Defence.
I do not visualize the committee as a committee to get information for propaganda purposes or to make political capital. I visualize the committee as a responsible committee, one that would realize the implications of the international situation and whose members would use whatever knowledge they had for the purpose of assisting the defence department in the best interests of the country. I believe the cabinet should give serious consideration to the matter.
Of course, in 30 minutes one cannot go over the whole white paper, but in reading it it seems to me that the greatest difficulty facing the defence department today is manpower. I think that is pretty well pointed up on page 19 of the white paper, and I should like to refer to paragraphs 59, 60 and 61 where I find the following:
59.	During 1955 the R.C.N. enrolled 3,088 officers and other ranks and wastage totalled 2,671. . . .
60.	The army's total enrolments last year were 5,937; and net wastage, 8,222. . . .
61.	During 1955 the R.C.A.F. enrolled 8,153 officers and other ranks and wastage totalled 6,573.
I am sure the minister will agree with me that a system of enlistment or induction where the total enrolment for the year is fairly well offset by the wastage leaves much to be desired. To me it indicates that there is something wrong with the examinations and the aptitude tests that are given when these people are taken into the services. In the three services-army, navy and air force-your total enlistment was almost offset by your wastage or people

that are going out. I therefore believe that the government is going to be obliged to take a straight look at this question of manpower.
Comparisons are made all the time with respect to the progress made in the Soviet union, and it is closely related to this question of manpower. Of course, being a dictatorial set-up, the Soviet union call people in, set the courses and the period of enlistment, and I will wager that there is not much wastage in their forces. If we are going to take the Soviet union as the yardstick on the question of manpower and on other questions, we must rethink this whole question through as to how we are to be able to meet the efficiency of a country where two or three men make the decisions from which there is no appeal, where you do what you are told and where decisions can be made fast. That is the question we must face in the future and there must be a great deal of rethinking on the whole subject. As indicated by the white paper, I think this question of manpower is a fairly serious one. Of course, we must not forget the recommendations being made by General Simonds right across the country to the Legion and so on. Maybe he has something. However, I just want to leave with the minister the thought that he has on his hands a fairly acute manpower problem with respect to keeping the services up.
On the other hand there is a great deal of thinking we must do with respect to this whole international situation. We send visitors from Canada over to the Soviet union, including Mr. Duncan and others. They come back here and they write pamphlets and deliver lectures in which they point up the efficiency of the Soviet system, the progress they are making in the air, with respect to guided missiles, up-to-date planes and all that kind of thing. As I said before, if the Soviet union is to be taken as the yardstick in these things and if we are to be expected to compete, these people who are making these speeches and writing these pamphlets must go all the way with it. The apparatus of the Soviet union controls everything in the country. All of the profits of industry, agriculture and everything else in that country go to the state. Three or four men can blueprint what is going to be done and make the decisions, and they have the money to spend. The thing that Mr. Duncan and these other people are not telling us is that in the Soviet union the profits that go to industry in this country are available for distribution in the field of the development of armaments, social services, and all of these things. If we are going to take the
Supply-National Defence Soviet union as a yardstick and are going to try to keep up with them in the field of efficiency, then much of the profits that go into the coffers of industry in this country must be used for the purposes for which the Soviet union is using them. That is the thing they are not telling us, and that is the difference.
With respect to this question of war, may I say this. For the last three years I have been personally convinced that there is not much danger with respect to a global war. First, I am sure the United States will never start it and I am reasonably sure we will not and Britain will not, but we have to keep our guard. My belief is that the Soviet union is more afraid of war today than the western world, and she is afraid of it for this reason. The Soviet union has extended far and has taken over many countries. She has taken over the whole of Europe right into East Germany and she is tangled up with the Orient; she is mixing in with the Middle East. Today, the Soviet union is like the fly that captured the flypaper; she is there and she is stuck on it. She has to police and maintain armies in all of those satellite countries. I am reasonably sure-and I am sure she is sure-that if an over-all shooting war started tomorrow the same machinery would be underground in those captive countries that was there when Hitler subjugated them. A shooting war tomorrow would cause a revolution right from East Germany back into the Ukraine. I am sure she realizes that and she does not want a shooting war.
I believe the new look in Russia is a new policy. I do not believe it is a tactic this time. I believe we should recognize the fact that an over-all global war would mean a counter revolution as far as Russia is concerned, which might spread right through the whole of that country. That is the reason for the change from the cult of the individual to the collective administration that Bulganin and Khrushchev are setting up today. I am reasonably sure of that but, on the other hand, there is a new war and it is a trade war.
The Soviet union realizes that if she is to survive there can be no shooting war. She is doing her best to offset that at the present time. I believe her efforts for peace are legitimate and she means it. I believe she thinks-and I think she is on sound ground -that if she can put over this program of peaceful coexistence and go into a trade war with the west and use the weapons of economic development, mutual aid and social change, in time she is going to be able to beat us in that field unless we recognize the fact that we have to get into that field and match wits with her.

Supply-National Defence
I do not believe in this business Of giving away the resources of the country to other countries on a relief basis. I do not believe you can buy friends in that way. I do not believe that aid to any of the countries, including countries under the Colombo plan, if we are giving it away, is going to do us any good. I think the main question in the countries to whom we are giving aid is one of self-determination. I think that is the one disturbing factor in the world today. The whole continent of Africa is uprooted. Do not forget, it is not a new thing. The prejudice is there and it goes back for hundreds of years. They want to run their own show. The same thing is true in Algeria. That question is 125 years old and it is not going to be settled with guns. That is another point of unrest. It is true in Israel and in the Arab countries. That is another see-saw thing that will have to be settled. The giving of stuff to these people, in my judgment, is not going to buy the settlement; it is not going to buy them any more than it bought Tito. Today he has gone back to his blood brothers. I am not objecting to it. He has the right to make that decision. The fact that the west made loans to him and was good to him during his period of trial did not make any difference.
I believe the question of self-determination has to be settled. On the question of mutual aid, if those people want aid from us or from the United States, let them make application for it and it should be given on a basis of either a loan or an investment, and they should be allowed to run their own show in their own countries.
Of course, we have to continue our defence spending. One of the reasons why I should like to see a defence committee established is that we might be able to iron out those difficulties in that committee and send the collective judgment of a large group from this house back to the heads of the defence department. It would do the heads of the defence department good to talk to the members; it would do us good to talk to them. We would get much valuable information and when the minister's estimates came before the house next time perhaps that information would place us in the position where we in this house would be helping the minister to put over a program that we knew something about.
I am not going to speak at length on this particular problem, Mr. Chairman. I merely wanted to express these three or four points that I have made. Before I sit down I urge the minister to give consideration to the setting up of a parliamentary defence committee on a permanent basis with liberal
[Mr. Gillis.l

terms of reference and with powers to compel the attendance of responsible officials. At this very moment a United States senate committee has powers to compel responsible officials to testify and it is conducting a comprehensive investigation into certain aspects of the United States defence program. The Canadian parliament has always been denied this right despite the billions that have been spent for defence purposes. I know for at least four years on end previous to the minister's taking over, the Leader of the Opposition and I were two members of the house who hammered on this question of a continuing defence committee, and I think it would be one of the most valuable assets of the minister's department.
I am not going to go into the question of weapons. I do not think any of us knows too much about it, but I will say this. A plane on the assembly line today is obsolescent before it is off the line. That has been the history of development in the air.
Another point I should like to make is that Canada has not the kind of money needed to match an arms race with the United States and the Soviet union. We just do not have that kind of money, and that arms race is going to go on and on. The Soviet union does not have to tax its people for it. It takes over wealth-producing industry in the country and applies whatever comes out of it to whatever it needs in the country. The United States is a huge, rich country. It has a lot of money but it is finding it difficult today to keep up with the expenditures made in the Soviet union in keeping equipment up to date. Perhaps we wasted a lot of money in building the D.E.W. line and the other apparatus that is supposed to warn us when planes come over. If you believe what you read in the press-and the white paper commented on it -it will be a push-button war. Planes will not come over. They will push a button and a guided missile will come across and land wherever they want it to land. Therefore, we may be wasting a lot of money in the development of interceptors, and so forth, because you are not going to intercept those missiles. They go above the stratosphere and appear from nowhere; you hear a bang and that is it. However, I think the white paper itself indicates, in so far as this country is in a position to do so, that the defence department is aware of what is going on. They set out all of the new techniques and all of the new equipment, and we are attempting to match it as best we can. But, as I said before, we do not have the kind of money needed to match an arms race with the United States and with the Soviet union.
I know we cannot change what is in the book. The money has been spent. We are

going to spend so much next year. The government is going to do it with certain techniques and on certain strategic projects and that kind of thing. This house has not enough information to be able to argue about it or make recommendations concerning it but there are two things I would like the minister to think about arising out of this debate.
First of all there is the question of manpower and wastage in the methods employed in bringing people into the services. That wastage clearly indicates there is something wrong with the examinations; maybe it is a rush to get people but we must not forget we are getting our people on a voluntary basis. In the United States there is a draft board and when your number is up you simply go. There is no exemption for baseball players, boxers or hockey players. You simply go in and do your bit in the defence of the country. In the Soviet union they do not even draft their men, they simply shovel them in and then select them and when you are selected for a position it is a case of doing it or else. There is no wastage there. The defence department in this country is faced with the problem of having to send teams out to travel across the country recruiting people on a voluntary basis. By and large the people we are getting in the services are those who are unemployed. There are not many who are vacating attractive jobs and going into the services.

I would like to see the minister make some pronouncement about a continuing defence committee. I think that is something that must be done. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity we have had during the present session to discuss the most important subject

Supply-National Defence that will come before the house both from the point of view of the amount of money involved and also from the point of view of the purpose for which the money is being raised.
The statement made by the minister yesterday added very little to the white paper. The white paper has been very correctly described editorially as a paper which says nothing. It says it in good English and in good French, depending on which of the two publications one reads, but the fact remains that as for stating a policy for Canada at this time the white paper might just as well have been brought out of the records of several years ago.
It is difficult to believe we are now called upon to discuss national defence in, the atmosphere in which it has been presented by the minister. Just in these past few months sweeping reorganizations have been announced in Britain and in the United States as well as in Russia. In fact, there have been two stages of substantial reorganization mentioned in Britain in the last six months. First came the white paper on December 21 last when a very frank appraisal of the situation was made and a general reassessment of the role of certain branches of the services was presented to the House of Commons and the people of Britain. Then came sweeping changes in the United States to be followed by still further adjustments based upon the extended inquiries that have taken place there. The Soviet union reduced the number of divisions and streamlined its force generally with a recognition of the modern concept of war which has emerged from the thermonuclear age.
There is little here to suggest that we are preparing ourselves for the kind of war with which we would be confronted if that war should come. God forbid that it should ever come. No one is under any misapprehension as to the horror that would accompany a large-scale war under present conditions. The dreadful fact remains, however, that these preparations are made with a realization and recognition that there could be war. It is, of course, correct to say that what is being done here, as in other free nations, is to seek to build military strength in a way that will prevent a general outbreak. That, however, does not get away from the fact that military preparation recognizes the possibility of war.
The estimates now before us call for an expenditure of $1,775 million. Further amounts probably will be added by the supplementary estimates which will be presented later. What have we before us to really tell us whether this money is being properly spent or otherwise? We really have nothing

but bland assurances which were not substantiated by the detailed facts which would make it possible for us to pass judgment on this vitally important question. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) warned us against a possible tendency to give credence to the smiling assurances which we are receiving. I should like to read his words. They express the view of the government in regard to the present situation, and I quote from page 5209 of yesterday's Hansard as follows:
To maintain the deterrent power of the free nations will not be an easy task, essential though it is to our survival. Paradoxically, as the existence of the deterrent continues to protect the peace, the continuance of that peace itself may tend to soften up the very deterrent force on which it depends, for it tends to give credibility to smiling assurances and friendly, folksy visits, all propagating the view that the day of world brotherhood has dawned at last, and suggesting that we can now safely set aside our defence programs, with their heavy costs, and concentrate on the much more pleasant task of raising our material standard of life.
Doubtless the statement that was made about the suggestion that we now disarm referred to a letter sent to the Canadian government by Premier Bulganin. I wonder if that was sent as a jest? I wonder what was the Canadian reply to the suggestion that we should disarm in the face of the massive forces possessed at this time by Russia. For a moment I was not certain what the minister was intending to imply when he spoke about giving credence to smiling assurances. What I think we should be on guard against is not only the smiling assurances from outside Canada but the smiling assurances from this government that all is well in our national defence preparations.
Let us examine what really are the facts. The only change of any significance that was mentioned yesterday was that the ten auxiliary squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force will no longer be part of our first line of defence. That probably is not very encouraging to units which had contemplated a role as part of the first line of defence. The reason for this decision is not made very clear, although the minister does say that the decision was reached reluctantly.
Let us see what has actually happened. Instead of ten auxiliary fighting squadrons which were intended to be part of the first line of defence in Canada and were intended, according to the statements made over and over again, to be equipped and trained for that purpose, we are now to have only six. One of the remaining four will undertake light transport duties. Another is to be used for the training of navigators. Another is

to be grounded and used for ground duties. The fourth is to be disbanded.
Instead of an increase in our air establishment this in fact means a decrease of four squadrons if the original intention of those auxiliary squadrons had actually been carried out. If special organizations were needed for the training purposes to which three of these four squadrons are now to be devoted those training units should have been organized for that purpose. It is true that the remaining six squadrons will be better equipped than they have been, but they are to be supplied with F-86s which are being withdrawn from first line use.
Why is this being done? This very question was dealt with on earlier occasions. The suggestion was made in earlier years that these auxiliary squadrons should be equipped with F-86s. I should like to read what the Minister of National Defence at that time said on April 15, 1953, as reported at page 3922 of Hansard. The Hon. Brooke Claxton, who was minister of national defence at that time, had the following to say by way of explanation as to why F-86s should not be supplied to these auxiliary squadrons:
The CF-100 was designed for the defence of Canada, and the F-86E was not. While the F-86E is unquestionably the leading aircraft of its type in the world today, it by no means follows that that is the ideal type of aircraft for the kind of operation we envisage as being necessary to defend Canada in the next few years. The range of this aircraft is not great, it has not full instrumentation and does not carry a navigator. Consequently anyone familiar with flying conditions in our north country would recognize that, while the F-86E would give a good account of itself, the losses would be high due to the fact that it might not be able to get back to its base again.
The subject came up for discussion the following year and at that time the Minister of National Defence, as reported on page 4991 of Hansard of May 21, 1954, had this to say:
There is another reason, and that is that these Sabre fighters are really not well suited for the air defence of Canada. They have a relatively short range, they have only one pilot: they have not a complete set of navigational instruments, and if they went into the air and got into a dogfight in Canada they might have great difficulty in getting back to their airfield. If we had our fighter defence in Canada staffed by Sabre fighters it would mean that we would have to have our airfields for fighter defence at least twice and probably three times as numerous as they are today because of the very much shorter range of the aircraft. Along with double or triple the number of airfields at present in existence we would have to have an increase in their attendant facilities, such as runways, oil tanks, hangars, married quarters, and everything else. An airfield costs about $30 million, and we would also have to double or triple the number of emergency landing fields.
If the Sabre fighters were not well suited for the air defence of Canada in 1954, what
Supply-National Defence has changed the picture today? If the F-86 was not suitable for the service referred to, why should that be the aircraft supplied to the squadrons which are to receive it according to the statement handed out yesterday by the minister? In an informative statement given to the press covering the statement made here in the house the minister said:
The Sabre aircraft which will be provided to 401 and 438 squadrons at Montreal, 400 and 411 squadrons at Toronto, and 442 and 443 squadrons at Vancouver will be the Mark 5. This aircraft is produced by Canadair Limited of Montreal, and has the Orenda jet engine. It is a high performance day fighter in the 600 m.p.h. class. It is expected that provision of the Sabres to the six auxiliary squadrons will begin late this year, and will extend through until next spring. The Sabres for the auxiliary will be flown back from the air division, where they are being replaced by the newer Mk 6s. All aircraft will be completely overhauled before being assigned to the auxiliary. In addition to the Sabres, these squadrons will receive an increase to the two T-33 jet trainers which they now have.
That statement by the Minister of National Defence indicates that aircraft which this house was informed in 1953 and 1954 were unsuitable for the service squadrons in Canada are now to be supplied under this new reorganization plan. Surely this present announcement indicates something of the confusion behind the announcements which have been made from time to time here in this House of Commons. In effect the minister says that squadrons which are not ready to take the air the moment an attack comes are going to be given aircraft which the Minister of National Defence who preceded him said were not suitable for the purpose for which they are to be employed. Then the minister said something else. The minister said that squadrons which are not ready to take the air the moment an attack comes will not get into active service. That in effect is what he said. In fact, his statement leaves the impression that those auxiliary squadrons are simply to supply the necessary replacement for the first line squadrons.
If that is so, then here is something that should be examined with the utmost care and in the utmost detail, and we should know what really lies behind this remarkable decision. Surely the Minister of National Defence is not making any suggestion that our over-all defence pattern is one that is ready for a full-scale war. He did say in his remarks yesterday that we were in a state of considerable readiness. These were his words, as recorded yesterday at page 5214 of Hansard:
Until recent years, we have never in our history had standing forces in peace time in anything like the numbers we have today.

Supply-National Defence
Then at another point in his remarks he said this, as recorded at page 5215 of Hansard:
Our services are well trained, well equipped, well disciplined. In character, in training and in resolution we have I believe as high a quality of serviceman as any country in the world.
I do not think that any hon. member of this house is going to raise any question about the accuracy of those statements, as far as the morale and as far as the standard of the men in our armed forces are concerned.
I have had the privilege, as have other hon. members, of visiting our air division in Europe. I have had the privilege of visiting our brigade in Germany. I have seen some of our naval units that visit other lands. Certainly we have every reason for pride in the young men and young women who are taking their part in those armed services. Our pride in their character, in their training, in their morale, should not, however, be used as an argument in any way to divert our attention from the basic considerations of organization, equipment and adequacy for the task in hand.
So far as the minister's statements are concerned, there is no evidence whatever of a truly Canadian concept of national defence related to the needs of defending this huge country of ours, the third largest country in the world, and at the same time accepting our share of the responsibilities under the United Nations and NATO.
There has been much public argument recently in regard to our defence forces. We have urged over and over again that the members of this house, through the proper channel of a committee of this House of Commons, be empowered to examine fully into this whole subject. I urged within a few days of the beginning of the present session that the whole question of national defence be referred to a committee of this house which would have power to call witnesses and to call for the production of documents and obtain other essential information. That request was flatly turned down. No explanation was given beyond the fact that the government had referred other matters to a committee on estimates.
Before I raised the question in this house,
I had written to the Prime Minister, making that proposal. His answer simply was to the effect that the government had already decided upon the four departments that were to be referred to the committee on estimates.
I made it clear then that the reference of the problems of national defence to the kind of muzzled committee on estimates with which this house has been provided would not in any way meet the situation. I pointed out that in Britain and in the United States,


the two countries with which we are most closely associated in problems of national defence, they are able to call senior staff officers and others before committees of the House of Commons and of the houses of congress, which obtain the facts upon which the members can then form judgments which are related to reliable information.
On the one hand we are told that we, of necessity, must follow in large measure the course that is followed in the United States as well as in Britain. We on the one hand retain organizational structures closely related to the British organization, and on the other hand are swinging substantially to equipment of the United States pattern. But one thing that is remarkable about this government and about the Department of National Defence is the measure of secrecy which they seem to think is necessary for the department of defence, which admits, quite frankly in this case, that its role is relatively much smaller than that of the corresponding departments in the United States and in Britain.
If it is possible in Britain to call senior staff officers before a committee there, and if it is possible in the United States to call senior officers before a committee of congress in Washington and have the most searching examination of the facts, then surely it should be possible for us to have a similar inquiry here which would give the members information to which they are entitled and which they have the right to demand.
Why all this secrecy? It is not to prevent the enemy from obtaining information. It is to prevent the members of this house from having the information that they should have. I should hope that the members on the other side of the house would exercise a belated measure of individual freedom and make some demand that they have the right to this information, because we recognize that it would be extremely helpful to have some indication from members opposite that they supported a demand that all of us have the kind of information we should have.
Do not let anyone suggest that information is not fully obtained there. I have in my hands the recent reports of the subcommittee on the air force of the committee on armed services of the United States Senate. I am not going to read from these reports, but just so that there will be no doubt as to the standing of the officers who are brought before committees for the purpose of inquiry let me read the list of officers who appeared before the inquiry as reported in part I between April 16 and April 20 of this year. Those officers were General Omar N. Bradley, Admiral Robert B. Carney, General Walter

Bedell Smith, General Carl A. Spaatz. Then, in part II, covering April 25 to May 2, we find that the following officer appeared: General Curtis E. LeMay, commander in chief, strategic air command. He was accompanied by all his senior staff officers. In part III we find that General Earle E. Partridge, commander in chief, air defence command and continental air defence command, appeared. He was accompanied by his senior staff officers. In part IV we have the following officers who appeared: Lieutenant General Emmett O'Donnell, deputy chief of staff, personnel department of the air force. In part V for May 10, we find that Major General Lee B. Washbourne, assistant chief of staff, installations, appeared on that occasion. In part VI we find that Lieutenant General C. S. Irvine, deputy chief of staff, materiel, department of the air force, appeared, accompanied by his senior staff officers. In part VII we find that General Otto P, Weyland, commander, tactical air command, appeared, and he was accompanied by his senior staff officers.
These inquiries covered the period from April 10 to May 10, and in that time the most searching questions were asked these officers. In fact, there was hardly a single occasion when the plea of secrecy was raised in regard to the discussions as to the comparative strength of the United States air organization and the air organization of Russia. Not only that, but they discussed in the most exact detail the quality of aircraft, the development of guided missiles and other details of that kind. Similar hearings have been held with respect to the army and the navy.
There we have complete frankness, complete disclosure. The members of congress in Washington are going to make their decisions based upon knowledge and advice of senior officers fully equipped to express their opinions and to state the facts. All this has a direct relationship to the change that has come about as a result of the threat of thermonuclear war, to which reference has already been made by the Minister of National Defence. I want to quote two or three paragraphs from an article which appeared in Fortune magazine written by Charles J. V. Murphy with regard to the effect of this threat of thermonuclear war and the balance of terror created by the increased strength of Russia in this field. I do so because Mr. Murphy has been recognized ever since the early days of the second world war as one of the most competent military observers in the free nations. This is what he says in Fortune magazine for March of this year:
The 1953 decision to concentrate U.S. military resources behind the nuclear deterrent has automatically decreed a new order ol military priorities,
Supply-National Defence the full effects of which are only now being felt. Overriding all others are the priorities attaching to the development of massive delivery systems capable of decisive retaliation and an air defence system capable of effectively checking the Soviet capacity for counter-retaliation. Because these two tasks by themselves make heavy demands upon the national pool of technical talent, not to mention the budget, all other military tasks are being progressively subordinated to them.
How far that subordination has already progressed may be judged by the comparative budgetary allocations for the three services in fiscal 1957, which begins in July: for the air force $16-5 billion, for the navy $9-6 billion, for the army $8-6 billion. Thus the air force, as the all-but-exclusive deterrent agent, now costs almost as much as the other two services together. Thus the old 1:1:1 ratio of military budgeting, which gave rise to so much controversy in the late 1940's has been shattered beyond recognition.
That statement, Mr. Chairman, discloses a position in the United States similar on a proportionate basis in some substantial measure to what has been taking place here in Canada. Then Mr. Murphy, in a later article on the same subject that appeared in the May issue of the same magazine, had this to say:
Now the big question is not merely whether still more money should be poured into the air force; rather it is whether, in light of the increasingly clear logic of the new weapons, the traditional roles and missions of the army and navy should not be radically redefined and the investment in them still further reduced. With the expanding deterrent sucking more and more technical manpower and money into its support, the question of how much can be spared for the traditional functions of the army and navy becomes increasingly urgent. For their separate dilemmas are caused in no small degree by the shift in emphasis from a strategy anticipating a long-drawn-out struggle across the face of the earth to one mustering resources for an overawing deterrent, which, should it fail to deter, would presumably win the first and decisive air phase.
This is not to say that the Eisenhower administration has accepted the "30 to 90 day war" theory associated with the most extreme air force elements. While conceding that the opening air battle, if it should come, will rapidly determine eventual ascendancy, United States military policy also assumes that the course of battle thereafter is unpredictable and that extensive, if not decisive, ground and sea operations may well ensue. Nevertheless, the main United States bet already clearly rests on the first phase deterrent.
I have read this, Mr. Chairman, because there also emerges from this concept of the overwhelming importance of the air force the recognition of the fact that we must not minimize the importance of the navy and, above all, of the army, which in the end, even in a thermonuclear war, would be called upon to occupy and hold territory no matter how devastated that territory might be. As Mr. Murphy says in this article, the course of battle thereafter is unpredictable and it may be that ground and sea operations may well ensue. He leaves the very clear inference that we must not be forgetful of the

Supply-National Defence vital role played by the ground and sea forces in anything that may be done.
The minister has placed much emphasis upon the deterrent effect of a thermonuclear war. I think there is now general agreement in every country that the likelihood of the use of thermonuclear weapons decreases as the menace grows. Certainly only a madman would let loose thermonuclear weapons when the terror of retaliation is recognized. Today it is realized that if Russia started a thermonuclear war the retaliation would be so terrible that Russia itself would be devastated to an extent that, with whatever desires for aggression they may have, they would not lightly contemplate that prospect. The very scale of destruction which both sides now recognize as a possibility and reality will unquestionably exercise a substantial restraining influence. But, Mr. Chairman, that does not mean that there might not be war and serious war which did not involve thermonuclear weapons.
I think it is well for us to remind ourselves that during the second world war both sides possessed the most terrible poison gas, far more terrible than any which had ever been used at any time in warfare. Both sides could also have waged bacteriological .var. Both had that dreadful equipment. God knows the war was terrible enough but both sides accepted the reality that gas and bacteria would not only destroy human beings but would completely disorganize ordinary domestic society on both sides to an extent that would be mutually destructive for generations to come. It is granted that the terror of poison gas and bacteria does not compare, in extent or horror, with the terror of thermonuclear war. Nevertheless there was a balance of terror in those fields.
We have actually seen the result of a balance of terror of that kind. The fear of retaliation kept those terrible weapons on the shelf. It did not prevent the most bloody, the most terrible and the most brutal war in all history waged as it was with conventional weapons. Is it not true that, under the dark clouds of a mutual fear of the hydrogen bomb, some nations might attempt ordinary wars with very serious consequences? In fact, we do not need to ask the question. Already some of them have done so. Russia did not hesitate to launch the attack in North Korea at a time when the United States had an enormous advantage in atomic weapons. Other local wars have been fought since that distant day in August 11 years ago when a new and dreadful era of warfare began.
Just as it was necesary for the members of the United Nations to make their contribution to a joint force to halt aggression in

Korea, it could be necessary for conventional forces to be required at some other point under similar circumstances. We hope that situation will not occur. What happened in Korea and the promptness of the action there undoubtedly has been a very effective deterrent in many areas. The threat remains, however.
Only yesterday western observers were startled when they saw the great military parade in Egypt when the full extent of Russia's supply of weapons was disclosed to the western world. From what was seen there it is estimated that over a quarter of a billion dollars in weapons have been supplied by Russia to Egypt just in this past year. The observers on that occasion saw heavy tanks, the most modern aircraft and other equipment which indicates what is happening in Egypt as in some other areas where Russian equipment is being supplied. Who can possibly say what dangerous possibilities will arise from that continuing supply?
We know what the communists can do. We know what they have done. They have developed a new type of warfare. Surely it is recognized that nationalism alone is not behind the trouble in Africa and Asia which has reached such explosive proportions at different times during these past few years. Undoubtedly national aspirations in Algeria have much to do with the bloody fighting that is taking place there and that is occupying the attention of so many thousands of well-trained French forces which could be used very well elsewhere. But certain it is that, just as in Kenya and elsewhere, communist agents have been fanning the flames of nationalism and stirring up hatred and discontent. That is part of their military program. Nationalist forces in different countries, stimulated by communist propaganda and supplied with Russian weapons, may well become fifth columns such as those which destroyed freedom in the early days of the second world war. I am not now suggesting that there may not be a great deal of merit behind many of the arguments for the recognition of the nationalist aspirations of many of the peoples in those countries where nationalism has come to such a boiling point. But I do say-without any thought that the statement can be challenged-that communist agents in every one of those countries have been fanning the flames of discontent in every way they can. It is therefore a matter of concern to us when we see great supplies of arms going to any country where there is a known cause of possible disturbance, as there is in the Middle East today.
Mr. Chairman, all this involves a broad concept of defence which goes far beyond

weapons and which goes far beyond the ordinary functions of armed forces but which unites in a great co-ordinated effort all the activities of our military, diplomatic and other forces to combat this planned assault on freedom which is being carried out in this way by Russia at this time. The point I wish to make, however, is that in these areas conventional weapons are being supplied. If discontent were stimulated to a sufficient degree, there could be a repetition of what happened in Korea. Then the free nations might be confronted not with the immediate threat of a thermonuclear war but with the threat of a conventional war waged under the umbrella of thermonuclear danger.
We have urged that great effort be devoted to our air force. Over and over again we have urged that there be an organization of mobile hard-hitting forces available for service anywhere in Canada or throughout the world that they might be needed. But those mobile forces, no matter how new in form they might be, would require conventional arms. It is to be hoped that we shall not forget that just as we need a navy to defend us against the threat of the tremendous Russian submarine fleet, so we also need an efficient, well-organized army to meet the continuing danger of what may be regarded as a conventional war in which today Russia has the enormous advantage of by far the largest number of trained and equipped troops.
Mr. Chairman, we have been called upon to examine these estimates. The fact is that we have not been permitted to learn what really lies behind the figures. What are described as the details do not give us the real details. Above all, they do not give us what lies behind the details.
It is certain that if a major disturbance came suddenly upon us, it would be necessary to turn again, as we have in the past, to our militia forces. The statements made by the Minister of National Defence in regard to their state of readiness are simply without relation to reality at this time.
I have had the privilege of visiting many units across Canada, as have other hon. members in this house. I have been associated for a very long time with the activities of the militia in Canada. The work being done by volunteer officers, N.C.O.'s and men is splendid, but it would be dangerous folly to pretend that they are equipped either for quick mobilization or even as training centres for large numbers of men if a dreadful emergency arose. The fact is that, in spite of the billions of dollars we have spent in the six years since the Korean war, there is not a single militia unit in Canada fully equipped, even under the limited establishment laid
Supply-National Defence down for these militia units. The infantry does not possess modern infantry weapons; the armoured forces do not possess modern armour; the artillery does not possess up to date military equipment. To deal just with the artillery to which I have referred, the Minister of National Defence yesterday spoke about the replacement of the 25-pounder by the 105 millimetre and of the 5-5 inch by the 155 millimetre. Mr. Chairman, that reference of the minister yesterday simply underlines the seriousness of the situation with which we are confronted. Large numbers of 25-pounders, with their equipment, have been withdrawn from our artillery units and they have not been replaced by the 105 millimetre. The same is true of the replacement of the 5-5. Our artillery units are not ready for mobilization; our artillery units are not ready to carry out effective training of the larger forces, as they should be, to fulfil their role. This is a situation which is merely a repetition of what occurred on earlier occasions, but on those earlier occasions we had not spent billions of dollars on national defence. We have been spending money on the scale of modern warfare and yet we have not even the basic equipment required for our militia units in this country at this time for their ordinary needs.
I mentioned before that at the beginning of this session I urged that there be a reference of the subject to a committee on national defence. At a later time I urgently requested the reference of the whole problem of national defence to a select committee on national defence. I explained at that time that a standing committee would automatically have the right to call witnesses, to obtain information, and to call for the production of documents, just as do the committees in London and in Washington. Surely, if one thing is clear above all else at this time it is that such a standing committee should be operating at this time so that we could actually get the facts lying behind these bald figures which are presented to us. After all, if it is justifiable to take nearly half of all the money collected in taxes from our people for national defence it should be their right, and it should be the right of their representatives, to know what the facts really are.
Yesterday, the Minister of National Defence quoted Clemenceau's famous words. I quote from what he said at page 5215 of Hansard, as follows:
It was, I believe, Clemenceau who said that war was top serious a matter to be left to the generals. The fact is, today, that it is far too complex and too technical a matter to be left to the amateurs- only professionally trained and experienced servicemen can cope quickly with the weapons and tactics of modern war.


That is the most serious indictment that could possibly be directed against this or any department of government, Mr. Chairman. What it really means is that the action of the government is not even being communicated to the proper officials under the system that has been set up. In other words, it is a case of the blind leading the blind.

Mr. Chairman, I am not giving blanket approval to this article; I disagree with many opinions expressed by General Simonds. That does not get away from the fact that it is not an expression of opinion; it is a statement of fact by a former chief of the general staff who was proclaimed as one of our leading soldiers by the present Minister of National Defence. When the minister asks me whether I approve I might well ask him whether he approves, in view of the almost blanket approval he gave publicly to the chief of the general staff at the time of his retirement. This, however, is a statement of fact with regard to administration. Now, I do not know whether or not it is a correct statement, but when the chief of the general staff-until quite recently a man who has been accepted by this government and others as an outstanding field officer-says in the June 23 issue of Maclean's magazine there is in effect a complete breakdown at the administrative level, I say we should have the opportunity to call General Simonds before a standing committee on defence and find out what the facts really are. I am not in a position to know whether that statement is correct. It is a statement of fact by the officer who held the senior position in the defence forces of Canada until comparatively recently. It is a statement of fact which I submit should be examined by the hon. members of this house in the only way it can be examined. I make more than a request, I make a demand on the Prime Minister, in the light of the importance of this subject, that now at this stage a standing committee on national defence be set up so that General Simonds and other senior officers can be called before that committee, and we might find out what the facts really are behind the veil of secrecy which surrounds the activities of the Department of National Defence at this time.
It was not only General Simonds who left the impression that all was not well. Surely we cannot without some knowledge of what

the facts are behind it pass over the statement of a man who was in the best position to know what the facts were, that senior civil servants can by deliberate and unwarranted stalling defeat the recommendations of the armed forces even though those recommendations have been approved by the cabinet.
Mr. Chairman, I think the Prime Minister should want a standing committee on national defence to inquire into that. I think the Prime Minister should want to know whether decisions of the cabinet are being stalled in the manner suggested by General Simonds in this recent article. I also think, in view of the very close relationship between the defence organization of Canada and the United States which has brought on to Canadian soil so many United States personnel in the air force and technical services and otherwise, we should be given the opportunity to learn what the facts really are in the only way we can do so, and that is by questions and answers from the man who made the statement. I think we should have the right to know if a paralysing barrier has been set up by the permanent joint board on defence. Who are the members of that joint board on defence? Who are the men who are, according to General Simonds, acting as a barrier to direct contact between the United States and the Canadian chiefs of staff? With all the interlocking relationships, there would be one of the most damning indictments that eould be levelled against any official in Canada if it were true. I most certainly place a qualification on this. I say that with this statement before us we have the right to know what the facts are, and I repeat I should think the Prime Minister himself, without any prompting, would insist upon a standing committee on national defence being set up immediately to find out if the decisions of the cabinet of which he is the head are being disregarded and prevented in this way.
Nor was it only General Simonds who made these statements; other senior officers have made similar statements. General Macklin, speaking on March 27, made this statement:
Canada needs a first-class army capable of competing with any potential enemy. We haven't got it. Our army in Europe, right under the guns, is ill-organized and ill-equipped, much like it was before world war II. Our army in Canada is likewise.
Those are the words of General Macklin, until recently the adjutant general of Canada, which he spoke publicly. There again is the kind of statement that calls for inquiry. Do not ask me if I support that statement. I am reading a statement made by one of those experts to whom the minister says he must look for his information and to whom
Supply-National Defence he was looking until a short time ago. I want to know whether or not that is a correct statement. I should think the Prime Minister would also want to know. I believe the Prime Minister has a compelling duty to find out through the channels of a committee, and I believe we have a compelling duty to demand the right to know, and the only way we can is through an inquiry before a standing committee that will have full power to call witnesses and produce documents.
General Macklin, of course, went further and spoke about our Chinese-wall concept. He said we were building up a static defence concept that was entirely contrary to the real needs of our defence organization. That may be right or it may be wrong, but by the ordinary processes of inquiry such as have been taking place in London and Washington we have a right to demand that the procedure be adopted which will make it possible for us to know. Do not ask, "Do you accept those statements?" What I say is, these statements are made by the experts upon whom this minister and his predecessor were called upon to rely. They are made by experts who are now free to speak. They did not just form these opinions upon their resignation, I feel sure of that.
Then we also have the statement of General H. D. G. Crerar, the wartime commander of the Canadian army, who on March 16 described Canada's present army as an attractive show-window with nothing on the shelves or in the storerooms. Mr. Chairman, that is not the opinion of an untrained individual. That is the statement of a man with wide experience who has kept himself closely in touch with what is taking place.
Why are these things being done? Why, for the sake of argument, is this manpower situation being dealt with in the way it is? Do not ask me what the manpower need is. The government has it in its power to find out. It appointed a manpower committee years ago which has not been permitted to carry out the duties assigned to it. What is more, the government has just recently made a completely new appointment. At page 305 of the defence estimates will be found the appointment of a civilian superintendent of manpower. Mr. Chairman, in the name of all reason, why does the department of national defence need a civilian superintendent of manpower? If the minister is relying on the experts he has spoken about, why not have the ordinary military relationship between his department and those who are called upon to form their opinions? Do not ask us; we certainly are anxious to express our opinion based upon information but the government is denying

Supply-National Defence us the essential information. The government says that all is well, and will not even bring these officers before a committee to find out what these facts are when the most challenging and damning statements are made by men in whom this government placed every confidence until a short time ago.
In the face of these positive statements by senior Canadian officers, can there be any doubt that those opinions are shared by other senior officers now in the armed forces who are not free to speak? Let us call them in, too. The officers who appeared before the committee in Washington are now in most cases serving with the army, the air force and the navy. Let us have the present chief of staff; let us have staff officers from the air force, navy and the army; let us have senior experts before that committee to find out what they say. Then we will have the kind of discussion in regard to national defence which is in keeping with the importance of this subject at this time.
The minister has said that there is no finality on this subject. There can be no finality. However, we want to be brought up to date; we are not being brought up to date by this white paper or by the bland assurances which we got yesterday. We know perfectly well that everything is not as it should be. We know perfectly well that our militia units have not the equipment they should have. We know perfectly well that we have not the kind of armed forces in being that are needed for the critical situation such as the world faces today.
It would be better by far to reorganize our forces and have every unit a unit in being, whether it be a permanent unit or a militia unit, than to have units partially equipped and in the same position they were in at the beginning of the second world war when in some instances it was necessary to wait for a couple of years before they were able to equip them.
We have had our lesson. Let us be done with smug complacency. We have the statement of the chief of the general staff, of the adjutant general and of other senior officers whose knowledge is very recent and who have made statements which should be examined without delay. We are not confronted with any question of Liberal or Conservative; we are not confronted with any question of government or opposition; we are not confronted with any question of mere debate or military estimates; we are confronted with the very survival of Canada, and nothing else. Uncertainty and half measures are not good enough. It is not good enough just to ask us whether we can make certain statements in
regard to requirements when we are not allowed to obtain information.
The government itself should take the initiative in this. The government itself should want information. If the government is really concerned to the extent which the minister has indicated, then there is no course open to them but to appoint a standing committee right now. We are going to be here several weeks and within the time that he will still be here every one of the senior officers could be called. We will call them before the committee and the government can call any experts it wishes to call and we will obtain the truth. We will obtain the facts. We will obtain what is really hidden behind the veil of secrecy at this time. Abstract figures are meaningless; figures and statements have meaning only in relation to the reality with which they must deal.
There is also for our consideration the wider concept of an entirely new type of war. The war which may take place will be, not only a nuclear war or a war of guided missiles but a war waged by conventional weapons just as was the Korean war, although there were atomic weapons always available and ready which could have been used. The day of the conventional weapon has not gone. The day of the infantryman, the artilleryman, the tank man and the other members of the armed forces in the army, the members of the naval units and the members of the air force, has not gone. There may be push-button warfare at some time and again there may not be, just as there was no gas warfare and no bacteriological warfare either in the second world war or in Korea.
We have a new concept of war. We have this new concept of the Russians' use of distant satellites armed in advance, not only from their own armament plants but from the great Skoda plant of Czechoslovakia and the great Teschen plant in Poland where mighty guns have been turned out for generations. The big berthas of the first world war were not made by Krupps, as was the general supposition; they were made by Skoda at Pilsen. So were many of the great guns that were used on the eastern front made in the Teschen plant in Poland. These great productive plants are available to Russia today and they are supplying deadly weapons of war to countries in disturbed areas where trouble may be caused.
Conditions in that kind of world add to the possibility of the new concept of war, and our thinking must be adjusted accordingly. We should have a Canadian concept, not a British or a United States concept. We need a distinctly Canadian concept suited for the real and immediate needs of the third largest

country in the world. No mere application of a British pattern or a United States pattern will suit a country of 3,750,000 square miles with only 16,000,000 people living in it. It must be the kind of force which will be suitable for immediate movement to any of the distant areas of this vast land of ours. It must be the kind of force which can move into the Arctic overnight, can move in there in a matter of hours. It must be a mobile, hard-hitting force making the greatest possible use of scientific developments of all kinds. That is the kind of force which would be the most helpful as a Canadian contribution to NATO.
I close these remarks by referring back to what I have said. I refer to the fact that it is not only in Canada that there is this tremendous demand for information. It is not very long ago that Field Marshal Montgomery, who has never felt unduly restrained in expressing his opinions, made this bold statement: Our organization for war is unsuited to modern times. We now have the statement of the chief of the general staff until a very short time ago; we now have the statement of the adjutant general until a short time ago; we now have the statement of the commander of the Canadian army in the last war who has had close and intimate contact with events since then. Their statements are all to the effect that there must be reorganization if our money is to be properly spent and if we are to have the kind of force we should have.
If there is one thing above everything else, in addition to what has already been mentioned, that should call for a committee of inquiry it is the surprising fact that exactly the same figure is used this year as was used a year ago as the requirement for national defence-$1,775 million. It just is not possible. Great Britain, the United States, Russia and other nations have carried out great reorganizations. For some reason they have been able to increase the efficiency of their forces with a decrease in expenditure. Yet we have exactly the same figure. We should not be asked merely to find out what particular items mean, we should be able to ask the staff officers why this situation exists. That would be the kind of debate that would be worthy of the urgency of this subject at this time.
I repeat to the Prime Minister, not a request but an urgent demand based upon the nature of these public statements, that there be a standing committee on national defence set up now. It could start to work immediately and we could have the essential facts in three or four weeks at the outside
Supply-National Defence and then the house would be able to continue a discussion of these estimates with the kind of information it should have. Whatever may have been the thoughts of the government before, when this government is confronted with the statement, by a man who was until recently its chief of staff, that the decisions of the government itself are being stultified by action within the department, then the time has come for this government to act in regard to the setting up of a standing committee which can really conduct an inquiry.
Again, however, let us remember this. It is not our support of a political party, whichever party we belong to; it is not the matter of an ordinary debate; it is not simply the figures that are before us; as the Minister of National Defence said yesterday, it is the survival of Canada that is under consideration, and I urge the Prime Minister to act in keeping with the solemnity of those words.

Mr. Chairman, after the thunderstorm eloquence to which the leader of the official opposition has treated us for the last hour, my few remarks will seem like the whisperings of a gentle zephyr that follows a storm. In view of the constantly changing international, political and technological situation, I fully appreciate the heavy responsibilities the minister has to carry and the complex and difficult nature of the problems he is called upon to face almost from day to day under these Circumstances.
Before proceeding, I must express my appreciation of the minister's courtesy and his personal attention to any problem I have brought to his notice. Whether it involved the problems of an individual soldier, of a unit in which I was interested, or of equipment or buildings or other things in general,
I have always found the minister willing to discuss them, to investigate things complained of, to report and to do what he could to remedy the situation, and I appreciate that. I must say that I have had occasions when I have had discussions with ministers and quite got the impression that I was conducting a monologue with a totem pole, but I have not found the minister that way.


I read the white paper and listened to the minister's speech carefully and with interest. I was particularly impressed yesterday with his concluding paragraphs, when he said, as recorded on page 5217 of Hansard:
Surely no one could look forward, with equanimity, to year after year of uneasy expectation of that dread day when the first H-bombs might fall. However futile our best attempts may have proved so far, we must keep on trying for disarmament. And we must come to grips with some of those central problems that have led to war: ignorance and hate, disease, privation and poverty.
For it is clearly evident-and it is on this note, and not a defence statistic, that I want to end my opening remarks to this committee-it is clearly evident that, for us and for the generations that will follow us into the wonders and hazards of this thermonuclear age, there must be some surer guarantee of peace, some less uncertain protection against disaster, than military might can hope to provide.
Man's inventive genius, which has sought out and set free the power of the atom, can surely make it serve and not destroy us.
I must say that I for one very much appreciate that spirit and that approach to the difficult times in which we live. I might say that the minister, when speaking, made reference to the departure of two members of this house for the centenary in London of the establishment of the Victoria Cross. I suppose he overlooked that another V.C., who has not been in our sense a member of this house but has been a member of the staff of this house for a good many years, I understand, also left with them. I am sure we all wish him, with the others, a very enjoyable and profitable time.
In my opinion the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, whose opinions on these matters I respect very much, made a most constructive speech, and I intend to refer to a few of his remarks later. I always think the member for Esquimalt-Saanich has a balanced approach, and while I do not always agree with him I think he is usually quite fair when he is dealing with these problems. I also thought my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo made a most lucid analysis of the situation from our point of view, and I think hon. members would be well advised to read his speech. I also listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River, particularly when he said, as found at page 5231 of yesterday's Hansard:
I believe that if the government would enlarge its defence program by adding a great ideological offensive we might be able to forestall the awful possibility that the great arms race might lead to another terrible conflict.
I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member suggest this, as it would mean using

the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as a propaganda medium for the government, and I am quite sure that no matter how carefully the government attempted to undertake that, it would very soon be accused of using the C.B.C. as an instrument of government policy. I do not think that is the right way to approach any of the problems to which the hon. member was referring at that point in his speech.
When I heard the hon. member make that proposal I could not help but think of my own father, who was a very strong Liberal. He disagreed with me politically very strongly indeed, but at the same time he was also, as a Liberal should be, a great democrat. He believed in freedom of speech and freedom of ideas, and he believed in the battle of ideas in a democracy. He was convinced that democrats could always win under those circumstances.
I remember one occasion just after the first world war when notices appeared in our village to the effect that a Mr. George Stirling, who later became a C.C.F. member of the provincial legislature, would arrive the next day on the steamer and would give a talk on the coming social revolution.
