Mr. Chairman, each year I enter this debate, like I believe every other hon. member who takes part in it, with graver feelings than possessed me the year before. As the minister said near the beginning of his remarks yesterday, no answer to the thermonuclear weapon has been devised and none is in sight. That is something by itself which I think must give us great cause to think. The fact that the manned airplanes that we have at the present time cannot guarantee that bombers carrying those missiles will not get over this country and be able to drop them, and the more fearsome threat which hangs over us that within a few years there will be intercontinental ballistic missiles for which there is no answer at all so far, I think combine to present a sort of frightening picture which makes it impossible to come to a discussion of the defence estimates in anything except a mood of some foreboding.
I should like first of all to say something about defence policy, as I did last year. Canada's defence policy is the basis on which our efforts must be, or at least should be, built. I have had, ever since the war, a very strong suspicion that the government was never very sure and definite what the defence policy is or what it should be. This feeling has, I must say, increased considerably in the past two years as a result of the fact that really very few changes have taken place in defence organization, set-up, and so forth; whereas the world has been in a great state of flux and what were valid defence concepts some time ago quite clearly


no longer apply. Now, defence policy, in so far as it is stated in any precise terms, is laid down in the annual white paper under "Defence Objectives". Prior to the last two years this statement was reasonably definite and straightforward, put down under headings 1, 2 and 3. The one for 1954 I have in my hand and it reads in this way:
The objectives of our defence policy remain the same as heretofore;
(1)	The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(2)	Implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or other agreement for collective security;
(3)	The organization to build up strength in a total war.
As I say, that was a reasonably definite statement. One might complain a great deal of the fact that the means being taken in organization and so forth, as I think was the fact, were not adequate to meet those objectives. It seemed quite apparent that whilst these were the stated objectives, the government really had no definite ideas as to how they were to be carried into execution.
Last year these objectives had become much less definite; they were fuzzier and more ambiguous, perhaps I might say, and I should just like to read them. This is from the white paper for 1955-56. At page 3 we find the following:
Canada's defence program continues to be planned for the immediate defence of Canada, for co-operation with the United States-
The first one was the same, of course. I continue:
-in the joint defence of the Canada-United States region-
That was much the same. It goes on:
-for co-operation within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization looking towards the provision of a collective force capable of deterring aggression, and for carrying out undertakings by Canada as a member of the United Nations Organization.
Well, as I say, these things might mean anything. They were fuzzy; they were indefinite. When we come to this year's white paper the fuzziness is carried considerably further and the amount of writing is very much increased, which I think is symptomatic of this year's white paper. As has been indicated by some other speakers, it is a well-written document. The contents are very good English, but this good English, in many instances, does not convey too much meaning. What we have this year on page 3, which again is really the start of the thing, is:
1. The aim of Canada's defence program and planning is to provide for the security of Canada.

That does not mean anything. If we had an army of cross-bow men here their purpose would still be to look after the security of Canada. If you have any defence forces their function naturally is the security of Canada. Therefore that first statement is, as I say, just a statement of the obvious and for any practical purpose it is meaningless and useless. It goes on:
Under present and foreseeable conditions this can be done most effectively by close co-operation with our allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and especially with the United States in relation to the North American area. Our defence plans must also include a capacity to carry out obligations that may arise out of Canada's membership in the United Nations Organization.
I have no quarrel with all these what you might call ideals, but I do wonder very much what definite plan or definite organization there is to carry them out. It is my contention there is not too much.
When we come to No. 2 of these objectives we have something that is perhaps a bit more definite. I am not going to read it all; but what it means in effect, I think, is that the Canadian government has accepted as its basic policy massive retaliation by the United States in the event of a full-scale war breaking out. I presume as a result of that its chief policy, as far as our own forces are concerned, is to tag them on to the military effort of the United States so they may be assisted in carrying out this policy of massive retaliation.
I agree that the threat of retaliation is a great deterrent to war, and I sincerely hope, as I think all of us do, that that threat, or at least the existence of an air force in the United States at the present time and one in Great Britain of bombers which have supplies of atomic and thermonuclear bombs, will serve the purpose of preventing any war taking place. Of course if the worst comes to the worst, it will mean that we are in a position to cripple the enemy at least as seriously as he has crippled us, and thus prevent the possibility of him overrunning the western world.
The rest of the white paper does not indicate, to my mind, any means by which we are going to be able to carry out this general objective, nor does it indicate what you might call any specific changes in military thinking, organization, and so on, which the complete change in the concept of modern war naturally forces upon us.
One subject in particular about which nothing was said is manpower. I think it is quite clear, from what little is contained in the white paper and from the little the minister has said at this time and previously, that there is no clear-cut plan as to how 67509-333
Supply-National Defence manpower requirements are going to be met. We have had a statement that there would be a maximum force of 120,000. The government has not explained why the figure was not set at 100,000 or 200,000 or at any other figure. In other words this apparently was just a figure decided upon for the sake of convenience because the government knew there were about that many men a year ago.
We have had no information concerning the allocation of the manpower as among the three services. We do not know whether the present allocation is correct or if it bears any relationship to the real need for manpower. I think the government owes it to the country and to this house to give us more definite and precise information concerning its manpower policy and how the present needs are going to be met.
The next matter concerning which we should have information is what reorganization of our defence forces is necessary to meet the three kinds of war into which we may be forced. The first is an all-out atomic war; the second is a conventional war, such as that fought in Korea; and the third is what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich referred to yesterday as a bush war, small, punitive expeditions in which we may have to take part.
I must admit that in his speech yesterday the minister did give us more information than is contained in the white paper. As was described in one editorial I read, the white paper might just as well never have come out as far as adding to our information with regard to our defence situation is concerned. The minister gave us some additional information, particularly concerning what changes would take place in the air force, the air crew, and projected changes in the army and so on. We are, however, still very much in the dark with regard to many of the important aspects of national defence.
As I said previously, this is a period of flux and change and it necessitates changes in military thinking and organization. The minister recognized that to some extent in his speech, because he said a committee composed of senior army officers was examining the organization of field formations for the army in order to make them more mobile and flexible. I am extremely glad that inquiry is taking place.
I do not share the view that has frequently been expressed in this house that military officers are always ready to fight the last war. This business of attacking the brass hats is almost a cult in Canada, you might say, the uncrowned king of which for many
5260	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence years was the former member for Temis-couata who has now been translated to the other place. This subject constituted the major part of his stock in trade. I was disappointed that the hon. member for Fort William brought out the subject of brass hats this afternoon and scoffed at them. I was also disappointed about the doubt as to their thinking ability which was expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay East.
Having met a considerable number of generals both during the war and since, I remain convinced that the majority of them are very able men. I would mention only two who I think prove the point very well. General Eisenhower, I think, is now acclaimed throughout the entire free world as one of the greatest men of this age. General Gruen-ther, I think, more or less commands the complete confidence of all NATO countries with respect to his ability and integrity. I mentioned these two men as examples. I think this matter of speaking contemptuously of brass hats and trying to convey the impression they are always thinking back to the last war and are not really intelligent people, and so on, is a pretty tawdry sort of thing and completely at variance with the facts.
As a matter of fact I think a good many generals and other senior officers in our armed services have been much more forward looking than the government, but they have been prevented from carrying into effect many of the changes they would like to have made. I believe that is indicated by the statements and articles we have heard of today, written by some of the senior officers who have recently retired.
As I said, I am glad to learn that the reorganization of the army is at least being studied now. I think the time is long overdue for us to take a long, hard look at our entire military set-up and organization. I do not believe the present organization is constituted to meet present threats. I do not believe the responsibility for that rests with the officers serving in the forces, but that it rests squarely on the shoulders of the minister and the government. They are the only ones who can make extensive changes.
The Leader of the Opposition has called for the immediate setting up of a committee of this house in order that we might have the actual facts placed before us by senior officers and others concerning our military situation as it exists at the present time. That is something I think should be done in the interests of Canada and in view of the responsibility of the government to this house.
In addition to that, as far as the long range improvements in our defence set-up and


organization are concerned, I think something else is necessary. I suggest a committee of inquiry or a royal commission-whatever you want to call it; some similar body at any rate-should be appointed and given some months in which to study the whole question of the organization of the Canadian armed forces, and that it be charged with the responsibility of collecting evidence not only in this country but in other countries in order that there might be some definite body of information on which this government and this house could base their thinking with regard to what our military organization should be.
This is the sort of thing which has been done frequently in the past as far as Great Britain is concerned, and it has been the means by which the whole military organization of that country has been changed from time to time. Perhaps the most famous military commission was the Esher commission as a result of which, I believe, the present general staff set-up in the United Kingdom came into existence.
There have been several other commissions in Great Britain. In every case it was found necessary, sometimes because of opposition on the part of people in the services or the general public, to appoint a commission to study the question thoroughly and for the commission to make its recommendations to parliament before any widespread changes could be put into effect.
We have had the same thing in this country to a limited extent. We had the Otter commission which studied the Canadian defence set-up and made recommendations which were adopted and upon which our military set-up prior to the first world war was really moulded or built. I would earnestly recommend or suggest to the minister that a commission of that sort be set up in order that the whole question of our military organization, in view of the great changes which have taken place in the world, may be studied and something better put in place of what is really a second world war organization which we have at the present time.
I would suggest further to the minister that in setting up that commission there are possibly three men who would make excellent members. I refer to the last three chiefs of staff of the three services, who have been retired. There could be two or three other men, such as Mr. Gordon who is heading the present Gordon commission. In other words there could be two or three civilians who had extensive experience in organization and in what might be called general business administration and things of that kind.

I should like to say something about the general organization, as I see it, of the Canadian defence forces at the present time. To begin with, headquarters is top-heavy, and by that I mean national defence headquarters in Ottawa. We were told in this article by General Simonds that defence headquarters would not work in the event of war. I shall come back to the general matter of the reorganization of national defence headquarters later. Before I do that I should like to say something about the three services themselves.
I do not feel particularly well equipped to deal with the navy, but I have done a considerable amount of reading on this subject. The chief function of our navy is antisubmarine. I think we all agree it should play an anti-submarine role. I have not heard or read of anyone advocating any other role for our navy. I have heard a considerable amount of questioning as to whether the set-up for this anti-submarine role, which is essentially the same as the set-up in the last war with the addition of an aircraft carrier, is adequate to carry out that role.
I think there is universal agreement that the new destroyer escort of the St. Laurent type is an extremely good ship, but it is a very expensive craft to build and therefore production is slow; it takes considerable time to produce these destroyers. This is indicated by the fact that this program was laid down some years ago but the first destroyer was several years late in getting into commission, much later than was projected when the plan was announced. Others will be later still.
I have heard it said quite frequently that while these are extremely good craft and the fact that we have a certain number of them is all to the good, they are not sufficient. It is said that in addition we need a number of smaller, fairly inexpensive craft which could be built rapidly as losses were experienced in the event of war. It is said also that there should be a more extensive use made of helicopters, perhaps both in connection with the smaller ships and the destroyer escorts. Surface craft alone are not going to be able to detect submarines as well or as satisfactorily as helicopters or ships aided by helicopters.
I have heard the fear expressed that with the type of navy we have the loss of a few of these exceptionally good but expensive and slow to build destroyers would cripple our navy to such an extent that it would be unable to carry out its role. It is for that reason particularly that a considerable number of more quickly built ships are necessary. Having had no naval experience I do not 67509-333i
Supply-National Defence feel competent to say whether these criticisms are correct, but they sounded reasonable to me. I think they should receive a considerable amount of study, not only by the minister and his naval advisers but by the commission which I have indicated should be appointed.
I come now to the army organization and the arms of the army. These are almost the same as they were during the last war. The minister made quite a point about the 105 mm. gun replacing the 25-pounder and the 155 replacing the 4-5 and 5-5 guns. However that does not readily improve the artillery of the army in the slightest degree. A number of gunnery officers-I understand some of them in the United States; in fact I was talking to one from the United States- believe that the 25-pounder is a better allround weapon than the 105 mm. They claim it is a more flexible and handier weapon. The 105 takes a little heavier charge and produces a little more punch at the end, but many gunnery officers consider that it is not likely to be as good a general, all-purpose gun as the 25-pounder. So the substitution of the 105 mm. for the 25-pounder has made no real improvement in the arming of the Canadian army. The only thing it has done has been to make it possible for the Canadian army to ride on the United States supply line rather than on the British, as has been the case heretofore. Whether that will be an advantage or disadvantage only the future will tell.
The Centurion tank is a new and approved weapon. I am glad they were secured and a considerable number are in use in our army. The only other improvement in our arms is the use of some mortars and rockets and the FN rifle. So it can be said that by and large, except for a limited number of improved weapons, the Canadian army in its organization and its armament is essentially the same as the army we had in the last war.
I do not think that is good enough; I do not think the minister thinks it is good enough, as is indicated by his speech. I am surprised that the situation has been allowed to go on as long as it has without any improvement. During the last three or four years we on this side of the house have called repeatedly for the use of more mobile troops, airborne and in armoured vehicles. Apparently there has been some advance in the thinking of the minister and the government, as the minister indicated in his speech that there was a new armoured vehicle of an amphibious nature which was going to be secured. When he comes to reply, or when we are dealing with the army, I should like

Supply-National Defence him to tell us how many of those vehicles it is proposed to secure, how soon they will be in the hands of units, and also if any of them will be given to the reserve army for training purposes.
Many people at one time or another have spoken of the army as being obsolescent, and so on. I do not believe there is any validity whatever in that contention. I do not think the army is obsolescent, or that it will ever be obsolescent as long as wars are going to be fought. As far as our defence thinking in Canada is concerned, we should work on the basis that it is going to be essential to maintain an army. At the same time I believe there is no question but that the old form of division such as we had in the last war and such as we have at the present time is not adapted to modern requirements. I believe that all the troops in an infantry division, or whatever kind of division you call it, should be carried either by air or in armoured vehicles. I think we must work in that direction as far as our army is concerned.
The information I have read in connection with the new German army is that it is all going to be either armoured or carried in tracked vehicles which will have good crosscountry performance. Whether you admire the Germans or not, you must admit that they have been extremely good military thinkers and organizers. The fact that they are going into a set-up of that sort should be sufficient to cause us to examine our position very carefully, where we still have our infantry battalions on their flat feet, in the same position they were in during the last war, with a certain number of trucks without crosscountry performance to transport them on roads. We must realize that in any future war there probably will not be roads on which to transport them. We must have vehicles with cross-country performance.

To return to this matter, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is fairly generally accepted that in the event of an atomic war troops have to be in fairly small formations. I think also it is going to be


essential that units, sub-units and even single detachments must be in a position so they can move rapidly about the country and be selfsufficient for, say, at least a week. Even in the last war we got to that, as far as antitank gun detachments were concerned. They had a ration box, sufficient petrol, a certain amount of water and all the ammunition they could carry. They could be set down and left for a week, and one did not have to worry about supplying them. It was probably only a small detachment of seven men to which that applied, but I think that will have to apply to other detachments, down to the infantry section and half-section. They will need to be carried in a vehicle which is armoured to some extent to give them protection against small-arms fire, and they will have to be equipped so they can live for a week or more by themselves without being supplied, because it is very doubtful whether the great supply trains of the last war and of previous wars-army service corps columns occupying miles of road, bringing up ammunition, food and all the other supplies- will be possible. As a matter of fact, most of the supplies will probably be air-dropped. Therefore the reorganization of the army, I think, makes it essential, to begin with, that these very small detachments, units, subunits and so forth, can each operate more or less independently. If most of a unit is wiped out, what is left can still operate without having to be supplied every day or two days.
That type of army organization is essential, I think, for atomic war, but also I believe it is a much better type of organization for any kind of war, whether it is conventional war or whether it is one of these bush fire wars. It is the type of organization which will be more mobile, more flexible and will give a better account of itself than the old type to which we have been accustomed is likely to do. In other words what I think we need, as far as the future is concerned, can be summed up in a few words: mobility, Are power, armoured protection for vehicles, and staying power, the ability to stay for a week or more without having to be resupplied. These things, I think, will be much more important in the wars of the future than numbers, and are what the reorganization of the army should aim at.
Now I turn to the air force. I think it is generally accepted by military thinkers of every country that it is in the last phase of its existence as a bomber-fighter force. In our case, of course, it is purely a fighter force. We have no bomber force. The general thinking is that in five to ten years the guided missile will have taken the place of the manned aircraft and, therefore, as a fighter-bomber force the air force will no longer have

a role to follow, though it will have that role for the next five to ten years, or something along those lines. As a result, I think the long-range thinking has to be directed toward the role which the air force is going to be assigned. What is going to happen, as far as it is concerned, when this five to ten year period is over? What has been its primary role no longer exists.
In the United States there is a very unseemly row going on between the air force and the army as to which one is going to look after guided missiles. I can quite understand that. The air force officers there see what the future holds and they want to retain their place in the sun and have control of the guided missiles. The army says they are just a form of artillery and belong to them. So the fight is on. Fortunately we have had no fight, in the open at least, in this country, as far as that is concerned; but it is one of the major matters of defence policy on which a decision needs to be made.
I think this house has the right to be informed as to what may be the thinking of the government, its military experts and others in regard to this very important matter. Whatever it may be, the air force, instead of having its present strategic and tactical role, is going to have quite a different place and a different role than has been the case so far. It is either going to have these guided missiles and thus become in effect the artillery of our armed forces or it is going to become a transport force to move men, supplies and so forth from place to place. Of course a change of that magnitude means that some forward thinking in preparation for it should be under way at the present time.
In any event, whatever is done as far as the air force is concerned-I have no fixed ideas on what should be done in that regard, but I am certain that these changes I have indicated are coming-whatever is done, as the strategic and tactical reasons for the separation of the air force and the army will have ended by that time, I do not think there is much question that there is no good reason to maintain that separation.
That leads me to the numerous suggestions that have been made, particularly by Field Marshal Montgomery but by many others too, in regard to the unification of the armed services. There has been a good deal of thinking about this matter by some eminent military men, many of them in the United States, including the present chief of their air force, who believe there should be complete unification of the three armed services and that there should be one service head. I think a move in that direction is probably inevitable in the course of time in order to
Supply-National Defence secure an efficient and effective defence force and, as I have indicated, I think we should perhaps be taking some steps toward it.
I find, Mr. Chairman, that I have taken about 15 minutes longer than I expected on this portion of my remarks. My remarks are more extended than I thought they would be from my notes, and as I do not wish to trespass on the indulgence of the committee I think I will give place to someone else and come back to this other matter later. It has to do with the reorganization of defence headquarters.

Mr. Chairman, during the years I have had the privilege of taking part in the discussion of the defence estimates I believe I have always begun with the complaint that we must deal with the important subject of Canada's defence preparations largely in a vacuum so far as detailed information is concerned. That has been true in the past and it is again true with respect to official sources of information. However, as other hon. members have stated during the discussion, considerable information has been placed before the public of Canada in recent years from certain high military sources, even though those sources are not quite official. Some of the information that has appeared in magazines such as Maclean's and Saturday Night, for example, has indeed been rather disconcerting.
I want to spend most of my time dealing with the air force aspect of defence, but before going into the details I should like to suggest to the minister that the stock answer we get from time to time, "not in the public interest", when we ask for specific information on certain aspects of military activity, the progress in recruiting, the new developments that are taking place in the various branches of the armed forces, is in my opinion a little bit overdone. I say so because I feel that if as the House of Commons we took the public of Canada into our confidence our armed forces would be much more efficient and our state of preparedness would be further advanced than at the present time.
To justify the assertion that we are adequately prepared to meet any emergency, we often refer to the continuing high level of expenditure which during the past few years has averaged some $2 billion a year. I am afraid that as a result of sloughing off responsibility in that way the ordinary citizen, when he writes his income tax cheque, which is quite substantial for the average Canadian, feels that he is making all the contribution that is necessary to the defence of Canada. It is the same sort of

Supply-National Defence situation that develops with reference to charity today. People who make contributions in response to various charitable appeals feel that they have discharged their complete responsibility by the financial contributions they make.
In my opinion the state of world politics today is such that the Canadian public should be made completely aware of precisely how inadequately we are prepared as a nation to meet an emergency, and also how inadequately the western powers as a group, particularly those associated with NATO, are prepared. The minister began his remarks yesterday in a rather ominous tone by referring to the threat of nuclear warfare, the threat of total warfare, for that is obviously what nuclear warfare means. If we are faced with any potential situation of total warfare that situation must be met by total preparation. We cannot have total preparation unless the people of the nation are prepared in every respect. We must not only be prepared by having a professional armed force, but the people must also be prepared psychologically, spiritually and from the standpoint of morale and esprit de corps in order to meet any possible emergency.
I think the real reason the answer "not in the public interest" is almost invariably given to questions that penetrate too closely to the heart of defence problems is that as a nation we lack any comprehensive policy. This year, as in previous years, I have searched the white paper in vain for any complete statement of Canadian policy in the face of the continuing world emergency. That is not merely conjecture on my part, because some of the statements that have appeared in articles in magazines have also suggested the same thing, that there is no co-ordinated effort to evolve a sound and comprehensive defence policy. That statement was made by General Simonds in his recent article in Maclean's magazine.
My suspicions in this regard are also aroused by the fact that defence expenditure for this year has continued at precisely the same level as last year, $lf billion, exactly the same figure as last year, which more or less suggests that the minister and his officials have made a rough guess as to what our defence expenditure needs might be for the next year and have decided to perpetuate the status quo so far as the estimates for the ensuing year are concerned. The charge of no policy is not new. As a young nation Canada has found itself in the same situation throughout our whole military experience.
I have been reading that very excellent history, "Six Years of War", by Colonel

Stacey, the first volume of which was published last fall, I believe. It deals with Canada's effort in world war II, and the point repeatedly emerges in Colonel Stacey's analysis of Canada's participation in the war and the period immediately preceding the war that there was no policy. There was no comprehensive planning. There was a hope and grope approach to the problem of defence. Perhaps that might be excusable in the period before world war II because we were living in a fool's paradise so far as our attitude toward any possible threat of war was concerned, but certainly we have had the harsh realities of the world political situation brought home to us in the years since the end of world war II.
I have here a few interesting observations by Colonel Stacey in this regard. For example, he refers to the minister of national defence during that period, the late Ian Mackenzie, at the imperial conference of 1937 opposing any extraneous commitments so far as defence expenditures were concerned. I came across this interesting tidbit. In 1936 the military chiefs of that day requested $250 million and received $36 million. Hitler was already on the rampage but we had our heads in the sand. In the appropriation in 1939-40, the year world war II broke out, the amount was precisely $60 million and Colonel Stacey in rather quaint language says that this produced a strong protest from the army. Of course, as I have hinted, the explanation was that we were still in the throes of a depression. Unemployment was still widespread. The public accounts still showed a regular deficit.
It is interesting to note that in 1938, on this same matter of defence policy, the then prime minister, the late Mr. Mackenzie King, wrote to all his colleagues in the cabinet reminding them of the recent deficits and emphasizing the importance of achieving a surplus and, if possible, some reduction in taxation before the next appeal to the electorate. I was most interested to find that any attempt by the military advisers of that day to set up an armament industry was turned back by the administration in those immediate pre-world war II days. Requests went forward from the chiefs of staff for the establishment of an armament industry right up to the outbreak of war, and those requests were continually turned back by the government. Of course, had the government accepted the recommendations of their military advisers the Canadian land forces in the second world war could have been armed with modern weapons from the outset. As it was, they made do for many months with the equipment of 1918.

I refer to these interesting extracts from the official history because they point out that we in Canada have never had a comprehensive policy toward military preparation. If it had not been for the quality-which we have heard mentioned in this debate several times -of Canadian young men who have volunteered for service in the two wars and in the Korean period of crisis, we would never have made such a magnificent showing as we actually made in the defence of Canada. It is quite true that Canadians have a strength of character that seems to bring out the best in periods of crisis.
If the world situation is as difficult and as black as the minister outlined in his opening statement, as is referred to in the white paper, and as is mentioned from time to time by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it is not enough to hope that Canadian citizens will rise to the occasion to meet any potential crisis that might be just around the corner.
Having had the experience of lack of preparedness for world war II and the unhappy state of affairs in the world that emerged following the collapse of the German reich, one would have thought we had learned our lesson. But we find that immediately after the cessation of hostilities the administration tried to revert to the pre-world war II period. We withdrew our forces from Europe and from Germany. We would not participate in the occupation of that country.
According to the official record, on October 1, 1946, the regular forces had been reduced to a figure below 50,000. The defence commitments for the fiscal year 1950-51 were $420 million. That was the year the Korean crisis commenced, and we made a complete somersault in defence plans. Panic ensued, and we embarked upon a period of defence build-up that has been referred to in this house from time to time. It was referred to by the former minister of national defence as "crash planning".
I think that just about describes all the contribution this country has ever made toward military preparedness. We have waited until a crisis was upon us; we have panicked; and we have indulged in crashplanning preparations. That is something which is tremendously expensive and tremendously wasteful; it is the sort of planning that produced the unhappy state of affairs outlined in the Currie report and which placed the armed forces of Canada in considerable bad odour for a long period of time. We are still not quite sure of where we are going, if we are to accept the opinion of the unofficial sources that have been discussing this situation in recent months.

Just before calling it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I should like to place on record a summation of the contemporary situation by the retired former chief of the army staff. He says:
Thus little dodging expediencies grow into vast incubuses and huge sums of money are committed on a "defence policy"-
Those words are in quotation marks.
-that has never been thought through in all ramifications and consequences, and is no more than a ramshackle expensive patchwork.
If I may call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I shall continue after the dinner recess.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was making the point that this question of lack of policy in defence matters is not a new thing in Canada. Actually, as a young nation we have never arrived at the position where we have met in a comprehensive way our defence responsibilities that have been increasing as Canada has assumed a role of increasing importance in world affairs. During the post-war era this particular aspect of public affairs has become a matter of extreme urgency.
The suggestion has been put forward, Mr. Chairman, that one of the reasons for our inability to outline a comprehensive program is the difficulties at the upper echelon of administration. It has been pointed out, for example, in recent statements by those who have occupied important positions in Canada's defence department that there is a bottleneck at the top; there is a break down in communication between the ministerial level and the level of chiefs of staff; there is a lack of liaison between senior civil servants and the other higher levels of command.
I recall that on former occasions during debates on the departmental estimates it was suggested that perhaps we should relieve the minister of some of his responsibilities by appointing a minister for air. That suggestion was made during the critical Korean build-up period. Following the Currie report discussion in the house there was an assistant minister of defence appointed. Now, these matters are in the realm of speculation, and I think the only way we can come to grips with the difficulty is by establishing a committee of the house that could meet from time to time and try to open up channels of communication and
5266	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence endeavour to bring our defence policy, which is a very important thing, into proper perspective at this time.
I do not want to spend all my time on policy; I want to deal specifically with the air force, as I indicated in my opening remarks. In matters pertaining to the air force I am glad to see in the white paper there is an indication that we are moving toward a semblance of a policy. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, before his departure from the house yesterday, congratulated the minister in this regard and indicated there is some evidence that the suggestions of the opposition have not been entirely without result; because the new policies, if you can call them that, that are outlined in the white paper are definitely based on suggestions that have come from this side of the house during discussions in former years.
The air force in Canada, because of the very nature of our geographic position, occupies a position of utmost importance in any Canadian defence policy. This is being recognized by the Department of National Defence, it is encouraging to note.
First of all, of course, there is the matter of personnel for the air force. Any branch of the service requires suitable personnel. I am not going to dwell on this problem. It has been mentioned by other speakers, but the white paper does indicate a high level of wastage which is not in the best interests of building up a strong, effective air arm. There appears to be a shortage of air crew. We have been trying to form additional squadrons for a couple of years now, and there seems to be a lack of the necessary trained personnel to equip those squadrons.
In passing, may I say that perhaps one of the reasons for the lack of interest of Canadian youth in the air force might be the relatively low level of incentive pay. This is a matter that has been mentioned in the house before. I believe it remains at the world war II level of $30 a month, regardless of the number of hours flown. Whether you are a chairborne pilot or a full operational pilot, you still qualify only for the additional $1 a day flying pay, which compares with something like $175 a month for the United States equivalent. Even in the R.A.F., where the service rates of pay are lower than the R.C.A.F., the flying incentive pay is at a much higher level. That, of course, is not the only factor, but it could be one of the reasons for the lack of incentive.
The main difficulty so far as personnel is concerned seems to be in the shortage of maintenance personnel. This is indicated by the increasing use of civilians to fill maintenance positions. In the realm of electronics,
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

private industry in Canada is growing by leaps and bounds. There is difficulty in retaining the personnel in the electronics field in the air force. The air force has tended to be a source of supply of qualified technicians in this particular area.
The problem of course, relates itself to the whole problem of personnel in Canada, where we are short of technicians of all kinds, where we are short of scientifically trained personnel. The difficulty comes up in almost all departmental discussions, and it is definitely sufficiently acute to require urgent joint action on the part of educational authorities and on the part of industry in co-operation with the government. If we are to have a comprehensive air policy we must meet the demands of personnel requirements.
Now, there is the matter of weapons. We have been discussing radar development on the North American continent. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, there is considerable misunderstanding concerning the function of our radar screen, which has been compared with the Maginot line complex, and so forth. There has been some criticism that unnecessary expenditure is going into the establishment of our three radar lines. Well, I should like to suggest that we have an excellent example of the function of a weapon of this kind-if you can call it a weapon; it is a defensive weapon-in the experience of the battle of Britain. Had it not been for the foresight of the pioneers in this field-they called it radio location in those days-the first of the few would not have succeeded in practically destroying the power of the Luftwaffe and winning the battle of Britain. They were able to do so only because they worked in close conjunction with the radar network that had been established around the United Kingdom.
Therefore I am one of those who believe that the radar installations are a very necessary and important development in any comprehensive program of air defence at this time. True enough, there are defects that cannot be overcome. We cannot detect highflying aircraft; we cannot detect low-flying aircraft. These defects were present during world war II, yet they did not offset the overall effectiveness of the screen.
The main criticism in this regard has been brought to bear because of the feeling that we have reached an era when we are faced with the immediate prospects of intercontinental ballistic missiles. But so far as any information I have been able to get is concerned, it would appear that the I.B.M. warfare, as it is called, is some 10 years away. I do not know whether the minister will agree with that figure; but if it is so you

have a 10-year interval in which the more orthodox air force defence is going to be required, and particularly the policy emphasis today on massive retaliation.
Massive retaliation seems to be the strategy of the west. If that is so I would agree, Mr. Chairman, that it is essential that Canada make its maximum contribution in fighter aircraft, because in the massive retaliation strategy it is going to be necessary for any potential bomber threat to penetrate deeply into the North American continent. Even a flying time of two or three hours makes it possible for conventional fighter aircraft, if we can call the CF-100 and the CF-105 conventional aircraft-the latter is not off the assembly line but it is more or less a conventional type-to intercept a considerable number of attacking bombers. Perhaps the best argument in support of our radar program is the fact that the D.E.W. line in particular would make it possible for our retaliatory forces, the strategic bombers, to get airborne and attempt to break through the enemy defences and at the same time give us time to get the fighters airborne to meet any onslaught from the enemy. I think we are moving in the right direction so far as our air defence policy is concerned. The CF-100 and the F-86 are admittedly obsolete and the sooner we can get the CF-105, which will be in production shortly, off the assembly line the better will be our defence position air-wise.
This leads me to make just a brief comment on the importance of the air industry to Canada. Canada is a natural country for the development of a strong air industry. We are a young nation and we are on the verge of tremendous development, particularly in the northern regions. In similar manner air power is just in its infancy. We are on the threshold of tremendous achievements in the air.
In the past the advances in aviation have come largely from the impetus that has been provided by military development. We in Canada have been gently ushered into the air age. We have the nucleus of an air industry, but I think there is a fundamental weakness in our approach to the establishment of an air industry in that our emphasis has been largely on the military aspect. Admittedly, as I have already indicated, that is where the initial impetus comes from; but the very nature of the Canadian problem, with its huge distances and with its potential in the north, suggests that we should be developing an air industry which provides a nice balance between military and civilian needs.

As I see the situation we are very deficient in the civilian aspect of this particular development. Even in the air force, as far as I have been able to determine, we are not moving forward too vigorously in developing a strong transport command; in fact we have been marking time in recent years. Perhaps that is because we are waiting for new types of aircraft to emerge; but it seems we are in an ideal position, Mr. Chairman, to combine a military production program and a civilian production program with a modified form of the Bristol Britannia type of aircraft that will be in service in a comparatively short time. This Bristol Britannia is primarily a civilian transport which is being modified for military purposes. I have the specifications here but time will not allow me to discuss them in detail. I would, however, point out that the Britannia has proven itself a very economic and effective interim transport aircraft. As we move toward the jet age, it is a transport aircraft that could serve in various capacities in Canada on the transcontinental route. Its runway requirements are relatively limited as compared with the pure jet transport, and certainly it could play a major role in the opening up of the north, particularly with the establishment of the numerous airfields in connection with the D.E.W. line.

I believe we were caught short in the D.E.W. line development. If we had planned very carefully, taking into consideration the special needs of Canada, we would have been in a position to have a very strong civilian air industry at this time.
There is another aspect of the necessity of co-ordinating civilian and military needs. The minister spoke of a mobile striking force as one of the objectives of air policy. That is another suggestion that has been put forward repeatedly by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. He is one of those retired generals with a very flexible attitude toward the changing demands of defence today. Any effective mobile striking force, in addition to being transported across the ocean by
5268	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence means of Bristol Britannias-if that were the type of aircraft adopted-would require air transport facilities to make it possible to deal effectively with any enemy lodgments in isolated areas of this country. That would demand a smaller type of aircraft, and again we have an industry in Canada producing an aircraft very suitable for that purpose. I am referring, of course, to the Beaver and Otter produced by the de Havilland Company. These planes have established fine reputations in the field of small air transports.
As has been said repeatedly, we have to balance the demands of total nuclear warfare with the demands of conventional warfare, and if we are going to have an effective air defence policy-we are moving toward it timidly-we are going to have to think in terms of completely air portable-not airborne but air portable-mobile striking force, as we on the side of the house have continually indicated. That, of course, is going to mean a much more effective and comprehensive transport command operation than we have at the moment.
One further thought on this matter of a Canadian air industry. It is a subject which I bring up regularly. I am not alone in harping on this theme; it is a theme that has been picked up in many areas in Canada. The most recent exponent is another retired general who has been making statements that should be listened to with considerable interest by the government.
I refer, of course, to General Worthington, who is in charge of our civil defence organization and planning. He has been saying repeatedly in recent days that we must avoid the building up of these huge city areas which are flowing over and absorbing the surrounding rural areas like the tentacles of an octopus, swallowing up the fruitful agricultural land as in the Niagara peninsula, for instance. This is occurring at such a rate that according to a C.B.C. program last Sunday evening-"In the Shadow of the City," I think it was called-if it continues to absorb fruitful agricultural land at the present rate there will be none left in that area in 10 years. There are 50,000 acres left now and we are absorbing it at the rate of 2,000 acres annually. That of course is due to the high concentration of industry in certain areas.

Mr. Chairman, in making my contribution to the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of National Defence I must at the outset plead guilty to a lack of technical knowledge which some hon. members seem to possess. I do not think I have ever seen one of these famous CF-lOO's, nor would I recognize it if I did. However, the Department of National Defence takes almost half the income of the federal government; therefore I am pleased to see more members taking an active interest in exactly what is happening to this vast expenditure of public money. As an ordinary citizen of Canada I am interested in what will be the effects of government policy in relation to the subject of world peace.
I am often asked back home to give some measure of explanation as to what the government actually uses this almost $2,000 million for, which they supposedly spend for defence. I do my utmost to explain that it is the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence to do everything possible to protect us from whatever hostile action we may be called upon to endure as a result of the activities of another nation.
I was a little disappointed the other day when I read the British United Press dispatch which reported that the people on the west coast of Canada had been subjected to radioactive rainfall. On the orders of the day on June 15 and June 19-I did not

f)Ut this question to the Minister of National Defence because I thought the matter was so important that it should receive consideration at a higher level of government than the head of one department-I asked by whose authority Canadian citizens were subjected to what might have been a dangerous radioactive rainfall, and I asked also what measures were being taken to assure Canadian citizens that things of this nature would not happen again. We did have the assurance in a news dispatch that the amount of radioactivity in the rain which fell was not harmful, but we have no assurance that on another occasion in the months and years ahead we might not be faced with disaster from other explosions which could be harmful. I say this because of the reports by scientists as to what may happen, and I look to the Minister of National Defence to supply me with an answer to the problem.
I feel it is the primary responsibility of the minister to protect the Canadian people from the actions of another nation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare replied that the Canadian government had not participated in any decision in regard to the thermonuclear explosion which took place about a month ago. If the Canadian government did not take part and was in no way responsible for that incident, then I feel it is up to the Canadian government to make representations to the authorities who were responsible in an effort to avoid what may some day be a serious situation. I am told that the scientists themselves are never sure at the time of one of these explosions how far-reaching the consequences may be.
Before saying anything more about the department I should like once again to place on the record my attitude toward the Department of National Defence. I made the following statement to the house on November 19, 1953, as reported on page 164 of Hansard of that date:
For the record I should like to make it perfectly clear here that at this stage I do not oppose but rather endorse the use of force which may be necessary for the maintenance of law and order. But such force must be exercised by some authority which is higher than those who are involved in the argument. As long as the United Nations is the United Nations and not the Soviet union or the United States I am in hearty agreement with the use of military force by that body for the maintenance of world peace.
Recently there occurred an incident in connection with which we felt most keenly the lack of a United Nations defence force, and I refer to the severe tension which obtained, and to a great extent exists even today, in the Middle East. At the height of that crisis the leaders of Canada, Great Britain and the United States seemed to be at a complete loss as to what action they should 67509-334i
Supply-National Defence take if the situation became worse. I am sure we are all glad that a conflagration did not take place at that time, but that incident revealed the urgent need for some plan of action on the international level being established before we are in the middle of a crisis.
The minister and the member for Esqui-malt-Saanich referred to that incident. However, the member for Esquimalt-Saanich also pointed out that when the Korean incident occurred we were really not prepared, and the United Nations as an international force was really not prepared and not in a position to meet the situation. It was only because we were fortunate enough to be able to engage in some delaying action that the forces of the supporting members were rallied and a longterm defence against aggression was undertaken.
If we are spending almost $2,000 million for our national defence we might as well give some serious consideration to having at least some of that money devoted to an international police force whose responsibility it will be to be ready for any little emergency that may arise; and little emergencies, as we know, can sometimes involve the whole world in armed conflict.
I also realize that Canada as a nation is too weak to have a defence policy of its own. We cannot act unilaterally; it would simply be a complete waste of public funds. If we are ever involved in a major world struggle, Canada alone cannot even defend her own shores. Therefore military organizations may be necessary. I have indicated that I would prefer to see that military co-ordination under the auspices of the United Nations. That may not be entirely realistic in the world in which we live, and we therefore have our NATO organization.
As I observe what is happening in the Department of National Defence, I get the feeling that Canada even today is still pursuing, for the major part, a unilateral defence policy. I will admit that there is some co-operation with our neighbour to the south and some of our NATO allies. However, the basic assumption still seems to be to build up a national defence force. I feel that the major emphasis should rather be on making our fair contribution to a united effort on the part of the western democracies, and making our fair contribution to world effort on behalf of maintaining peace.
Then I think the shift from the military to the economic front in the so-called cold war has particular significance for a country such as ours. I believe that in this shift may well lie not only the salvation of world peace but

Supply-National Defence our own economic salvation. We are producers of many of the basic needs of the world, and some of them we have in excess. We do not know what to do with the surpluses we have. If the cold war were really fought on the economic front, we would find ample markets for all the products that Canada is now producing and also for those we would be able to produce if we made a sincere effort to produce to win, as some years ago we made an all-out effort to produce to win the war.
We have the Colombo plan, to which we make a contribution. We make a contribution to the refugee assistance program, the United Nations technical assistance organization, the world health organization and various other international organizations. However, our sum total of contributions on the economic front thus far has been most insignificant when placed in relationship, first of all, with our ability to donate and, second, with the expenditures on the military side of the battle for men's minds.
We have at the present time a department of national defence which spends over $100 per annum for every man, woman and child in our nation. The ordinary people of Canada have a right to know something of what they are getting for this continuous, heavy expenditure of public funds. We had an explanation given us by the minister the other day in regard to the radar lines, which are among the most expensive of our defence expenditures. As recorded on page 5211 of Hansard, he said:
These are projects of great difficulty and magnitude-costly, but we believe worth the cost. For they will buy us time-time to get the big United States deterrent force of bombers with their nuclear weapons winging away on their missions should the need arise, time to get our defences activated, time to prepare our people for impending attack.
I must agree with the first reason the minister gave for the existence of radar lines. Anyone knowing the world situation and looking at the globe will have to admit that. However, I must take exception to the last part of his sentence, when he says these radar lines will give us time to get our defences activated, time to prepare our people for impending attack. I believe the minister is not telling the whole story when he says that. I believe that when these radar lines were first initiated that was possibly the greatest reason for initiating them. However, if the minister has, as 1 am sure he has, read the statistics on the performance of modern aircraft, of the Russian accomplishments and so forth, I think he will have to admit that none of our radar lines-the mid-Canada line, the "Pinetree" line or the distant early warning line, will in any shape or form, for any practical purposes, be able to warn our people to


prepare themselves to resist the effects of an attack. That has become outmoded. A sentence like that five years ago might have been acceptable to this house, but in 1956 it is no longer valid.
With many other members of this house I went to the military installations at Fort Churchill; I believe it was a little over a year ago now. There is one recommendation I should like to make in connection with that. Wherever possible I think the efforts of the Department of National Defence should tie in with the national life of Canada, so that more Canadians will know that we actually have a department of national defence and so that as many Canadians as possible will at least receive some of the benefits of this large expenditure of money.
When I refer to Fort Churchill, what I have in mind is this. Here we have the military camp supplied with purified, running water, all the sanitary services you could wish for, hydroelectric energy and so forth. Yet only a very short distance away we have the old Fort Churchill where the ordinary civilians live, and they have no sanitary facilities, no water supplied to them. None of the amenities that are available and supplied to the armed forces there are extended to the civilian population. I feel that with a little bit of extra money the people living there in Canada's north could receive some of the benefits of having the military camp next door.
I heartily endorse the need expressed by my colleagues and also the members of the Conservative party for a committee on national defence. I think the Canadian people and the members of this house in particular are not nearly well enough informed about what is happening, what is being done with the money. I realize there may be need to maintain some of these expenditures on the secret list. However, when you look at what is happening in other democratic countries of the world I doubt very much whether you will find another western nation where the minister in charge of defence is given authority to spend $1,700 million odd and nobody is able to investigate to find what is actually being done with the money.
Furthermore, I maintain that there is great need for more public relations efforts on the part of the minister's department. The ordinary taxpayer back home sees only the advertisements inviting him to don a uniform. He sees very little else of what is being done by the Department of National Defence. I think a percentage of the money could very well be devoted to an explanation to the public, in ways by which other departments of the government well know how to obtain


public sympathy and understanding, of what we ought to be doing; and if the public find out we are not doing what ought to be done they will be able to do something. No one wants to be responsible for endangering the safety and welfare of his own nation, yet people are not supplied with the information that is needed. Therefore one can sympathize with people when they begin to raise serious questions.
Finally may I say that my main purpose in rising tonight was to say that I believe that unilateral defence for Canada as a nation is outmoded, useless and a complete waste of money. In my opinion we must collaborate with the other nations of the western world, and especially must we bear in mind that at no time shall we harm the possible collective security that may well be set up some day for the safety of the world by the world-wide organization, the United Nations.

Mr. Chairman, this evening I should like to deal briefly with three different subjects coming up or not coming up under the estimates of the Department of National Defence. The first is the program of defence research and development. If hon. members will turn to page 339 of the estimate book they will find that the minister is asking for defence research and development in the current fiscal year the sum of $79,032,389. Last year he asked for $52,578,000, so there is an increase in that particular estimate of practically 50 per cent. Of that increase of over $26 million, more than $21 million, according to the estimate book, is for the acquisition and construction of equipment, the total amount required for that purpose, including the increase, being practically $50 million. That is by far the largest part of the defence research and development vote.
Incidentally, it is interesting to recall that in the fiscal year 1954-55, two years ago, the amount asked for research was $50,400,000, and that in each of the two preceding years it was only $42 million. Therefore we are now being asked to vote almost twice as much for research and development as was voted in the years from 1952 to 1954. This amount of $80 million is a very large sum of money. I remember sessions just before the war when $65 million was voted for the whole Department of National Defence, and everyone thought that was a very big expenditure. Now we have $80 million for this one particular portion of the work.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that parliament should have some check on this expenditure for research and development. This session we have set up a committee on nonmilitary research, but so far as I know there has never been any committee of the house
Supply-National Defence with the power to inquire into the ways in which the money voted for research was being expended by the Department of National Defence. I realize that some of the work must of necessity be secret, but even in the days of the war there were committees with the power to go into many expenditures of a similar type, and I see no reason why there should not be a committee of the house at the present time. Probably the committee on national defence suggested by my leader this afternoon would be the one to undertake that work. We have the position today that very large sums of money are being sought for defence research without any adequate check whatever on the part of the members of the house.
In connection with the research and development program I ask the minister to tell the committee the cost to Canada of the "Velvet Glove" project. We find it referred to on page 35 of the white paper. It seems to have been at least one of the main projects of the defence research board, and the white paper has this to say:
Shortly after the inception of the defence research board in 1947, a small group of the board's scientists began studies in the guided missile field. In recognition of future Canadian needs for special air defence weapons, and under arrangements with United States and United Kingdom authorities, the board concentrated on the family of air-to-air missiles.
Apparently that was to be Canada's field, air-to-air missiles.
In 1950 it was decided to undertake a practical but experimental Canadian project. The prime purpose of the project was to build up within the board's staff and throughout Canadian industry a team of scientists and engineers capable of developing and producing guided missiles in this country, while familiarizing officers of the Canadian services with problems and techniques involved in using such weapons.
Then the report goes on to say this:
126. Known as the "Velvet Glove", this project has resulted in the training of some 400 specialized personnel in Canada, and has been accompanied by the development of facilities for research, testing and evaluation of guided missiles. A limited number of missiles are being produced, particularly for testing and training purposes at the R.C.A.F.'s establishment at Cold Lake, Alberta. Canadian industry has made progress towards developing design and manufacturing capability in this complex new field.
By the way, earlier in this particular section of the white paper it is stated that the principal increase in the vote for research and development is directly related to anticipated expenditure in connection with the CF-105 airplane, and the guided missile program. Hence even in this vote that we are considering tonight there is a great deal of

Supply-National Defence money presumably for this guided missile project. Then the white paper goes on to say this:
127. On the basis of this preliminary work Canada is now working out arrangements for the production in this country of a United States type of air-to-air missile, in order to make Canadian interceptor aircraft better able to perform their role in the air defence system.
That white paper does not make it clear that the "Velvet Glove" project has not been successful. The minister did that when he spoke yesterday. As reported at page 5214 of Hansard he said this:
The pioneer work was done on the "Velvet Glove", which so far has fully come up to its original specifications, However-
And this is a very big "however"; this is the part that indicates that the whole project has not been a success.
-because a somewhat similar United States missile is of more advanced design, it has been decided not to adopt "Velvet Glove" for operation use, but to modify the "Velvet Glove" program and go into production of one of the Sparrow series for use with the CF-100 and the CF-105.
It would appear that at least some and probably a great deal of the money that has been spent on the "Velvet Glove" project has gone down the drain. I ask the minister, when he replies, to tell the committee just what amount of money has been spent on this "Velvet Glove" program.
Again, another point in connection with research is this. What consideration is given to long-term defence requirements before any particular research project is authorized? I ask that question because General Simonds raised it in his article in Maclean's magazine. I do not know whether or not General Simonds is right in all his statements in this magazine, but in any event he is one of the most distinguished soldiers this nation has ever produced. Probably we have never produced a finer field commander. He has served as chief of staff and, as we all know, he served with distinction. His statements must carry weight. Even if they do not carry much weight with the government I am sure they do with the Canadian public as a whole. These statements he has made should be answered by the Minister of National Defence in the course of this debate.
General Simonds has this to say. He refers to the navy and the air force. I do not know whether he left the army out because he is an army man, but at any rate in this particular part of the article he says this:
Thus the navy and the air force, which sustain a large sector of the shipbuilding and aircraft industries (the latter existing almost entirely upon defence expenditures for research, development and construction), are encouraged to embark on new projects, without too searching a consideration of whether what is being researched, developed or


constructed necessarily represents the most valuable contribution to defence in the longer term.
Then he gives two examples. He says:
Thus, having regard to its timing, the wisdom of embarking upon the development of the CF-105 fighter is open to serious military objections. It should be abundantly clear by now that the ground-to-air missile offers the only prospect of eventually counterbalancing the existing ascendancy of the offensive in terms of aerial warfare. If, as many believe, there may be a dangerous time gap to be covered by some form of defence, after existing fighters are obsolete and before a really reliable ground-to-air guided missile is available in operational quantities, then it would have been both more sensible and economical to have adopted a prototype fighter developed by the U.S. or Britain as a gap-filler rather than to embark on an expensive venture of our own, the product of which at best will have a very short, if any, useful operational life.
I stress these next words:
The combined vested interests of the air force, the aircraft industry and defence research scientists, burning with zeal to participate in a project they could call their own, coupled with the known desire of ministers to maintain a defence effort with a strict manpower ceiling, swept aside any opposition to this venture.
He also has a similar criticism of the mid-Canada line. He says this:
The mid-Canada line with its "McGill fence" equipment could be justified as a stop-gap measure if there should occur an appreciable time lag between its completion and the completion of the D.E.W. line. It is difficult to understand what useful part it can fulfil in a defence system based upon guided missiles, which is a "must" of the not-distant future, if an even adequate defence is to be provided against offensive air power. The United States has pressed the construction of the D.E.W. line with such vigour that it is for serious consideration whether the arguments for construction of the mid-Canada line were not powerfully influenced by a desire to put to use gadgetry-
He uses this word "gadgetry" several times throughout the article, presumably referring to the defence research board.
-evolved in Canada at considerable effort, rather than considerations of what would provide the best defence, most capable of adaptation to new weapons as they evolved.
Those criticisms may or may not be justified, but they should be answered fully by the Minister of National Defence. It just may be the case, Mr. Chairman, that in our defence research effort we are spreading the money over too many projects. It might be better to concentrate and also to be a little more careful about giving directions for the start of any particular project.
The second subject I should like to mention tonight arises also out of the article by General Simonds. I refer to the present status of the permanent joint defence board. The general points out in the article-and correctly, I think-something in connection with the permanent joint board on defence;

that is, of course, the Canadian-United States board. He points out as follows:
The existence of the permanent joint board on defence adds further confusion to the direction of our military affairs.
He seems to think it is a fifth wheel to the coach. He continues:
This organization came into being during the period of world war II when Canada was a belligerent and the United States was still neutral, and at that time was a useful instrument for obtaining some co-ordination of measures for North American defence. Now it simply acts as a barrier to closer liaison between the Canadian and U.S. chiefs of staff, and is redundant in so far as its military activities are concerned.
That is a very serious charge in view of our association in the defence field with the United States. Then General Simonds goes on:
But the chairman has a more ready access to senior cabinet ministers than have the chiefs of staff. Whatever the terms of reference may be, many of the expressed views of ministers bear the unmistakable imprint of the influence of an intellect more remarkable for its bias toward pseudoscience and gadgetry, than for its record of sound military judgment.
These are rather harsh words about the Canadian chairman of the joint defence board; but what is the function of this board today? Why is there need for a permanent joint defence board working on its own when we have such close liaison between the two countries in military affairs? Surely that work should be done by the Canadian chiefs of staff rather than left in the hands of any outside board. What useful purpose is this joint defence board serving at the present time?
Then my third and final subject is this, Mr. Chairman. We read in the very first paragraph of the white paper about Canada's defence objectives. These are the broad defence objectives. This is the way the paragraph reads:
The aim of Canada's defence program and planning is to provide for the security of Canada. Under present foreseeable conditions this can be done most effectively by close co-operation with our allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and especially with the United States in relation to the North American area. Our defence plans must also include a capacity to carry out obligations that may arise out of Canada's membership in the United Nations Organization.
I point out that there is not one word in this paragraph, or in any other paragraph in this whole white paper, about the commonwealth, not one word about co-operation with the commonwealth in defence matters. Surely one of the main objectives of this nation in defence matters should be co-operation with the other nations of the commonwealth. Young men from these commonwealth nations fought side by side in two wars. In
Supply-National Defence the first war we had Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, we had troops from India, beside us time and again in France; and you could have no finer troops beside you, as I think the minister will admit.
