Even Field Marshal Rommel, in the second world war, repeatedly expressed his great admiration for the New Zealand division, and considered them the finest troops facing him in North Africa.
In the second world war our young men fought and died beside young men from the other nations of the commonwealth. I saw, and probably the minister did too, the first young air force recruits under the commonwealth training plan go through Vancouver from Australia. Many thousands of them came that way, trained here in Canada and then flew their machines with our own Canadian pilots and navigators. Young men of the commonwealth saved civilization just a few years ago, and for a year they stood alone to do it. In 1941, with the exception of the short time that Greece was able to stand up against the nazi hordes, the British commonwealth stood alone and saved civilization.
And, by the way, things might have been different if it had not been for the young men who were trained in Canada in the air. It might also have been a great tragedy if the original plan of this government not to allow any British or other commonwealth airmen to come here and train had not been changed, and changed very suddenly.
This was what happened just a few years ago. Just 11 years ago these young men from the different nations of the commonwealth were fighting side by side and saving civilization. A few years ago in Korea we had the commonwealth division; yet today co-operating with the commonwealth is not even mentioned as an objective of the Canadian government in defence matters. I suggest to the minister that the present is a very appropriate time for something to be done about this failure. The Prime Minister is going to London within the next day or two to attend a meeting of the prime ministers of the commonwealth. Let him at that conference raise some of these defence questions.
For example, why should Canada not extend her present air training plan to include young airmen from other parts of the commonwealth, from the nations of the commonwealth that do not belong to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the Australians, the New Zealanders, the South Africans, the Indians, the Pakistanians and the Ceylonese; any member nations of the commonwealth
5274	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence that wish to participate in this training plan. At page 14 of the white paper I find the following:
At December 31, 1955, under the NATO air crew training plan carried out at R.C.A.F. establishments in Canada, a total of 1,741 pilots and 2,130 navigators, including observers, had graduated and a further 939 trainees were on course. These trainees have come from Belgium, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, The Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Turkey and the United Kingdom.
Why not extend that scheme and allow young men to come from other nations of the commonwealth?
Why not co-operate with the other nations of the commonwealth in the guided missile field? The British have proving grounds for guided missiles in Australia. They have done a great deal of work in that field. Why should not our Prime Minister suggest at the conference that all nations of the commonwealth which wish to do so should participate in a common guided missile project? These are the type of things which will have to be done. If they are not, if we just allow the commonwealth to drift along without facing some of the realities in the world today, I doubt very much whether it will continue in existence for a great deal longer.
Our defence effort and our defence expenditures are designed to prevent world domination by the communists. That is the one reason we are spending all this money in Canada for defence. If war comes, we all know that it will not be only in the North Atlantic treaty area; it will be a global war. It will be just as hot on the Pacific as it is on the Atlantic, and perhaps quite a bit hotter. Some of these commonwealth nations will not co-operate with NATO, but I believe they would be willing to co-operate with the other commonwealth nations in the fields which I have suggested. Co-operation of the commonwealth nations in a third world war might well be the deciding factor.
I urge upon the government, particularly on the Prime Minister and on the Minister of National Defence, that in our own interests we should leave no stone unturned to further co-operation among the commonwealth nations in defence matters at the present time. Some may not be willing to go very far; others might be willing to go the whole way, but let us at least do our part to further that type of co-operation among this group of nations which give allegiance to a common sovereign, our gracious Queen Elizabeth II.

Mr. Chairman, this house is fortunate in that its membership includes hon. members with great experience in all branches and at all levels of the armed services. I have personally met among its members those who


have held ranks ranging from general down the line to buck private. They probably bring to bear on the problems of national defence as much personal experience and knowledge of these problems as any group of men anywhere in Canada.
Many of the matters which are discussed under the estimates of the Department of National Defence do require a high degree of technical knowledge and practical experience in one field or another of the armed services. Those of us who may not have had such extensive experience in that field are well advised, I think, to leave to the experts commentary and discussion in their field of special knowledge. On the other hand, there are many things which affect the Department of National Defence and many matters which come under its control which are reasonable grounds for discussion, comment and examination by anyone in this country, whether he be a civilian or an armed forces expert. The very extent of the department's budget, the amount of money it spends, would seem to bear out the truth of that statement.
I remember reading not so long ago that it takes the wool from 20 sheep, I think it is, to clothe a soldier; and I thought to myself at the time that to keep that man in the field it also takes the hides of about 30 taxpayers. I do not think, Mr. Chairman, any citizen of Canada objects to the expenditures on national defence where they are justified and properly made, but I do think every citizen of Canada and every hon. member of this house has ample justification for questioning certain of those expenditures and for feeling at many times that these expenditures are made without proper explanation to this house and sometimes, when we do find out how and why they have been made, without sufficient justification.
We must remember it is extremely likely the world will remain in a state of armed preparedness during our generation. There seems to be little likelihood of any major change in international relations in the foreseeable future that would permit us to beat our swords into plowshares. If, then, we are to remain in a state of armed preparedness, and if we are to be asked year in and year out to spend millions of dollars for national defence, we will have to adjust our thinking and approach to the subject of these expenditures to a peacetime concept rather than a wartime concept. By that I mean that a certain attitude of mind toward such expenditures which may be allowable and understandable in time of war should not be carried into peacetime. In brief it is the attitude that says, "Hang the expense. We must do the job at any expense and

immediately, even though we are not absolutely sure the job needs to be done immediately".
That is the attitude one expects when one is under the gun, but it is not necessarily an attitude that is justified when the world is in a period of cold war, of planning and preparing for what at any moment may break out into a hot war but a hot war which certainly has not arrived as yet.
Second, in this matter of changing our attitude, Mr. Chairman, it would seem the necessity for the wartime attitude that everything connected with national defence, defence expenditure and all varities of activity in that field should be cloaked in secrecy may have to be altered. I do not think it is quite reasonable to expect the people of this country to continue year after year to willingly vote any amount of money requested by the Department of National Defence unless that department is prepared in peacetime to go further than it has to date in co-operating with this house in laying before it the details of many aspects of its operations.
It has been pointed out, and rightly so, that there are some things which should not be made public; but let me ask, Mr. Chairman, is there some marvellous capacity residing only with the armed services of this country which makes them the safe repositories of restricted information and renders a small committee of this house a doubtful repository for the same information?
Within this field of restricted information it might very well be said that all the details cannot be brought into the house and laid on the table in the full sight of every hon. member of the house and the press gallery. Through those channels, and correctly so, the information becomes the property of every resident of Canada no matter where his national or international sympathies may lie. But surely the type of committee which it has been suggested should be set up on an allparty basis could be taken completely and absolutely into the confidence of the Minister of National Defence and given all the information it required. Surely there are many, many aspects of national defence now kept under this cloak of secrecy which could easily and properly be brought into this house, explained to us and, if necessary, the accompanying expenditures defended before us. The best evidence of the government's unwillingness to do this has been their recurring refusal to refer the estimates of the Department of National Defence to the committee on estimates. Without labouring the point may I say that I hope the government will see fit to change this attitude at the next session of this parliament.
Supply-National Defence
Having made these general remarks I should like to deal for a few minutes with some of the expenditures of the Department of National Defence very much as a taxpayer of this country might see them. Of course I cannot touch on every individual item, but there are a few which seem to require some explanation. In one field, for example, the department seems to be engaging in operations which could be carried on quite successfully by private enterprise. Indeed, I think this is one of the weaknesses of any over-large government department. Eventually they come to the conclusion that as ancillary operations to their main purpose they should carry on a multitude of functions. They are quite sure they can do these better than private enterprise, and they insist on carrying them on without any attempt whatsoever to divest themselves of the responsibility.
As examples selected from the last report of the Department of National Defence we find that they are in the restaurant business in a reasonably sizeable way, in that in the year under consideration they sold over $64,000 worth of meals. Then we find that they are in the photographic business, because they sold over $81,000 worth of photographic supplies. Then we find they are in the laundry business, because they took in over $160,000 for doing laundry. I am quite sure that if I were prepared to dig a little further I could find a list of other items, but I give those as typical examples; the restaurant business, the photographic business and the laundry business.
Let us realize that these three things are by definition not operations which are carried out for the Department of National Defence as such, because had they been these sales would not have been made. What I have just quoted indicates the actual dollar revenue received by the Department of National Defence for sales under these various categories.
This raises two points. First there is the whole question of the propriety of the Department of National Defence carrying on functions which might very well be carried on by private enterprise. In isolated cases there may be some justification for this particular course of action, but I am not at all sure that it exists everywhere it may be pleaded. It is very easy to claim that one must operate a restaurant and serve meals, for example, if one has not gone out and made a series of honest attempts to find somebody to come in to operate that particular restaurant for the Department of National Defence.
Second, and this is perhaps even more basic, there is a difficulty, under this system

Supply-National Defence with the government engaging in operations of this kind and with their cloak of secrecy draped around them, of establishing whether the various activities of the department are really being effectively and efficiently and economically operated. I find amounts coming into the department under the various categories I have mentioned, but nowhere in the departmental estimates can I find any corresponding expenditures. I hope when the minister replies he will give us a little breakdown of what the costs were as opposed to these various sales. If we are going to be in business, if we are going to sell merchandise, if we are going to sell supplies, I think we have every reason in the world to know the details of the business we are operating. I suggest that by no manner or means is this classified information.
When we go on a little further we find that although education is completely a provincial matter the Department of National Defence is very actively engaged in educational activities, presumably at the grade school and high school levels, not only for their own personnel, although they have that too, but I submit specifically for the education of dependents. It may come as a surprise to many people that there are some 17,000 children attending schools operated by the Department of National Defence, and that those schools employ some 668 teachers from coast to coast in this country.
It must be admitted that if we set up a defence post in some completely inaccessible part of this country and ask men to go there with their families and there is no educational system in the area the government has a responsibility to provide educational facilities for those children. That I am quite prepared to admit. But where are these schools? Many of them are in major centres. In Calgary there is a school with 876 pupils; in Edmonton there is one with 303 pupils; in Shilo, Manitoba, not far away from a major centre- there are those from Shilo who would be offended if I did not indicate that Shilo itself was a major centre-there is a school with 648 pupils.
I come on down the list and find that at Petawawa there are many children of nonmilitary personnel who go to the regular schools of Ontario, but the army has set up a school with 34 teachers and 884 pupils. I could go down the list indefinitely, which I shall not do, and point out the major centres in Canada where these schools have been set up.
It may be argued that the department might suddenly develop a base and find that the educational facilities provided by the province are not sufficient, and they then

have to move in to meet the demand which they have created. However, I suggest that is exactly the type of mentality to which I have referred before, the mentality which says, "We will do it ourselves under federal government auspices rather than to seek the solution through the normal channels of free enterprise and the governmental system of this country at the provincial and municipal levels." If the government has a school to accommodate 800 pupils, they must have built the building. It seems to me that whether that building was built directly by the federal government or whether the federal government turned over the necessary funds as a municipal grant and had the building built by the school authorities of that area, it would have cost approximately the same amount.
It seems to me that the teachers who are teaching those pupils might just as well have been hired by the educational authorities of the province as by the federal government. It seems to me, and I think to a great many people in this country, that if the second course of action had been followed, the one which fitted this type of operation into the normal structure, the structure that Canadians as a whole would like to have in this country, rather than having the domineering and dominant control of the Department of National Defence we would have had a system that would be more satisfactory and that would better meet the needs and the demands of our Canadian civilization and economy as we know it.
Without going into details, although I have them, I would point out that the Department of National Defence is also in the housing business in a big way. It seems possible for all other areas of Canada, and all other segments of the economy, to build their own houses-very often, admittedly, with government loans.-but it also seems that the Department of National Defence for some reason must produce some 15,000 houses across this country rather than letting the free enterprise system, through the normal channels which are available to it, do exactly the same job.
We find the department in a number of other fields, and it shows how this mentality can gradually develop. Without going into the details I could tell the minister, for example, that his department needs many bookkeepers for the Montreal area, I imagine, for stores and so on. Did they think of arranging a contract with a local business college or anything like that in order to train these people? No.
I have here the civil service notice advertising for an instructor in bookkeeping to work for the Department of National Defence. His duties are exactly the same as those which

would be carried on by an instructor in bookkeeping in any commercial college or business school in this country. I shall just read the first part:
Under direction to instruct naval personnel in the principles and practices of bookkeeping; to assist in the preparation of training syllabi in the above subject; to draft and mark interim and final examinations . . .
I suggest that this type of thing is much better carried on through the normal processes. There are tens of thousands of bookkeepers in this country who received their education and training without the blessing of the Department of National Defence. If the department wants bookkeepers, it seems to me that the course for it to follow is to arrange with a school already set up to do the job for it.
Then you can go one step further and see again how this mentality expands and develops and moves ahead. I hold in my hand two pamphlets. They are interesting. They are well printed and effective. Inside the cover is the following statement:
The kind permission of the Royal Canadian Air Force to make the text of this training pamphlet available to the public is gratefully acknowledged.
I presume the pamphlets were previously restricted information. The title of one is "Beginning Hockey", and the title of the other is "How to Play Better Hockey." I am not opposed to the Department of National Defence encouraging its men to play hockey. It is a wonderful sport. It is a very good idea that the men should be encouraged and that they should be properly trained. But I suggest again that without the help or cooperation of the Minister of National Defence, there are tens of thousands of youngsters and young men across this country from coast to coast who have learned to play hockey and learned to play it extremely well. There are possibly thousands of those who also have read about hockey in pamphlets or books which they have bought at the corner bookstore, but here we have the Department of National Defence invading the publishing field and the sports field with their own pamphlets on how to play hockey.
Then we may go one more step, and perhaps this is the most interesting one of all. I hold in my hand a very well taken photograph of some 40 Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps cadets. They are in uniform, and parading in front of them is a man who would make a very good toothpaste advertisement, a very handsome man and well qualified man for his job. The reason he would make a good toothpaste advertisement is that he is smiling broadly. These Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps cadets are attending the Rosita and Deno dance studio in Montreal for dancing
Supply-National Defence lessons. As far as I can find out they are doing so under the aegis and blessing of the Department of National Defence. They certainly are in uniform, and they are certainly there in a body and, according to my information, they are certainly there as a national defence project. I think the minister could very well tell us something about this particular aspect of national defence work-dancing lessons for the cadets-and whether he plans to extend it into other fields and, if so, what those fields may be.
Let me make it very plain that I have no objection to ordnance corps cadets or any other men in the armed services taking dancing lessons. I. have no objection to them taking lessons in playing hockey. I have no objection to them having all the amenities open to them, because they have a hard, exhausting and demanding job; but I do object, first of all, to the government getting into so many of these fields itself as part of its defence operations. Second, I object to, in other cases, the government sponsoring certain types of activities-and I think perhaps the dancing school is a very good example- which are hardly a proper part of the work of the Department of National Defence.
I may be criticized across this country. There may be those who feel that we now have a government which must cover all these fields and even extend as far as that. Perhaps I am just a hard-shelled, unregenerate Tory, but I cannot bring myself to believe that there is any point in the Department of National Defence lining up its cadets of a morning and marching them down en bloc in uniform for dancing lessons.

There is a feeling on my part, and I think on the part of many Canadians, that this tremendous emphasis on security, necessary as it may be, may eventually find its way, as it has done in some instances already, into an invasion of our personal freedoms in this country as a whole and in this house.

But above all, Mr. Chairman, even though this is so, we must realize that these

Mr. Chairman, I wonder how this white paper is drawn up. Is it drawn up for the purpose of precluding one little peek at the expenditure of this money? I have ten full pages of notes on the minister's statement,

but after listening to him I ask, has his statement been designed to preclude, if at all possible, a single question about this blank cheque the government wants?
Oh, Mr. Chairman, let us not make any mistake about it. It is a blank cheque, because it is the identical amount that was signed last year in this very house. When you arrive at the figure, Mr. Minister, I wonder how you do it. To these men who go to work on that budget of yours do you say something like this: "Last year I got through $1,775 million, and if I could get it through last year I think I can do it again, and you will have that much money to play with. We complained about certain things last year. We brought them up in connection with the examination of these estimates. You say that is the reason you employ civilians, because then you do not have the additional expense of moving personnel. There does not seem to have been an explanation for it last year. Mr. Chairman, I recall that last year I read an editorial which said that the opposition must break through. I am not exactly sure what we are going to break through. This is the most illusory opponent that any opposition could grapple with. When I say that, Mr. Chairman, I am not referring to the minister personally in any way, but I say I am sure that he is surrounded by the hard crust and the hard core that Lieutenant General Simonds referred to in his article in Maclean's magazine.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    INQUIRY AS TO AMOUNTS ADVANCED TO DATE
speechtext: How can you be surrounded by a hard core?

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    INQUIRY AS TO AMOUNTS ADVANCED TO DATE
speechtext:
You ought to know, because you were fortunate in coming up from that hard core and landing in the seat you have now. You ought to try the other way of getting into this house; then you would find it a little more difficult to make the quips and cracks that you make.
But I say this, Mr. Chairman. I agree with my leader that we do not adopt these charges and say they are true. But when the ex-chief of your army staff makes charges like these we say it is time we had a committee appointed to investigate and find out as to their truth. I might say tonight, Mr. Chairman, that for my own part I would prefer it if perhaps some of the generals said these things before they retired.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    INQUIRY AS TO AMOUNTS ADVANCED TO DATE
speechtext: Hear, hear. So would I.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    INQUIRY AS TO AMOUNTS ADVANCED TO DATE
speechtext:
I would prefer it if perhaps the principle were great enough for them to say these things; if perhaps the principle were great enough for them even to risk the position they held, because there is no doubt about it that these things need saying. But let there be no doubt about it, Mr. Chairman; the evidence is here which requires an answer in only one way, and that is by a review of these expenditures before a committee of this house.
Mr. Chairman, that is all the time I have tonight. May I call it ten o'clock?
Item stands.
Progress reported.
